questions.question: What is the difference between verification and validation?
questions.answer: Verification is the process of checking that the software is built correctly against its specification - it answers the question 'Are we building the product right?'. Validation checks that the right product was built and that it actually satisfies the user's real business needs - 'Are we building the right product?'. Verification is mostly static and does not execute code: it includes reviews, walkthroughs, inspections, requirement traceability and static analysis. Validation is dynamic and requires executing the application: functional testing, system testing, regression and User Acceptance Testing. Verification typically happens early in the lifecycle, while validation happens once a working build exists. A simple interview mnemonic is that verification prevents defects and validation detects them.
questions.realTimeExample: On an e-commerce checkout project, verification meant reviewing the payment requirements document with the business analyst and confirming that every field, validation rule and error message was captured before coding. Validation came later when we ran the checkout flow in a real browser and confirmed a customer could actually pay with a saved card end-to-end.

questions.question: Explain the SDLC and its phases. What happens in the maintenance phase?
questions.answer: SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) is the structured process used to plan, build, test, deploy and sustain a software product. Its typical phases are requirement gathering, analysis and design, development, testing, deployment and maintenance. It can be executed through models such as Waterfall, V-Model, Iterative, Spiral or Agile. The maintenance phase begins after the product is released and covers fixing production defects, applying patches, adapting to new environments (OS, browser, dependency upgrades) and delivering minor enhancements. It is the longest phase in terms of cost and duration because real usage surfaces issues that were never anticipated. Testing during maintenance focuses on regression, bug fixing and impact analysis to ensure changes do not break existing functionality.
questions.realTimeExample: For a retail banking mobile app, once it went live the maintenance phase kicked in: we fixed a production bug where the OTP timer expired too quickly, upgraded the app to support a new Android version, and shipped a small loan-calculator enhancement every quarter.

questions.question: What is the STLC, and what are its phases?
questions.answer: STLC (Software Testing Life Cycle) is the structured sequence of activities performed by the QA team to test a product. Its main phases are requirement analysis, test planning, test case design and development, test environment setup, test execution, defect reporting and tracking, and test cycle closure. Each phase has defined entry and exit criteria so that the team knows when it can move forward - for example, test execution cannot start until the build and test data are ready. During requirement analysis testers identify testable requirements and raise ambiguities early, and during closure they publish test summary reports and lessons learned. STLC runs in parallel with SDLC, ensuring testing is planned from the very beginning rather than bolted on at the end.
questions.realTimeExample: On a food-delivery app release, our STLC looked like this: we analysed the 'apply promo code' stories, wrote 40 test cases, set up a staging environment with seeded restaurant data, executed the cases, logged 7 defects in Jira, and ended with a test summary report showing 96 percent pass rate before sign-off.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Agile and Waterfall models?
questions.answer: Waterfall is a sequential, plan-driven model where each phase (requirements, design, development, testing, deployment) must finish before the next begins, and requirements are frozen early. Agile is iterative and incremental: work is delivered in short sprints, requirements evolve, and testing happens continuously alongside development. In Waterfall, testing is a distinct late phase and feedback is expensive to absorb; in Agile, testers are embedded in the team from sprint one and participate in refinement, planning and daily stand-ups. Waterfall suits stable, compliance-heavy projects with fixed scope, while Agile suits products with changing requirements and a need for fast feedback. The trade-off is that Waterfall offers predictability and documentation, whereas Agile offers flexibility and earlier defect detection.
questions.realTimeExample: For a government tax-filing portal with fixed legal rules, the team used Waterfall with sign-off gates because the requirements could not change. For a startup social app, the same company used two-week Agile sprints so the checkout and feed features could be adjusted based on user feedback after every release.

questions.question: What are the different types of software testing, and which have you performed?
questions.answer: Software testing is broadly split into functional testing (checking what the system does) and non-functional testing (checking how well it does it). Functional types include unit, integration, system, smoke, sanity, regression, retesting and acceptance testing. Non-functional types include performance, load, stress, security, usability, compatibility and accessibility testing. Other useful categories are black-box, white-box and grey-box (based on knowledge of internals), and static versus dynamic testing. In my projects I have personally performed smoke, sanity, functional, integration, regression, retesting, exploratory and cross-browser compatibility testing, and I have collaborated closely on performance and security testing with specialist teams. Choosing the right mix depends on risk, project phase and the criticality of the module.
questions.realTimeExample: On an online insurance portal I ran smoke tests on every nightly build, functional and integration testing on the claims module, regression testing before each release, and exploratory testing around date and premium edge cases. Performance and penetration testing were handled by separate specialist teams that I supported with test data.

questions.question: What are black-box, white-box and grey-box testing?
questions.answer: Black-box testing treats the application as an opaque box: the tester validates behaviour using inputs and outputs without any knowledge of the internal code, so it focuses on requirements and user experience. White-box testing looks inside the box and exercises the internal structure, logic and paths - it is used for unit testing, code coverage and static analysis and is typically done by developers. Grey-box testing is a blend: the tester has partial knowledge of internals (for example, database schemas, API contracts or architecture) and uses it to design smarter test cases and locate defects faster. Black-box is the most common for functional QA, white-box is strongest for early defect prevention, and grey-box is very effective for integration and API testing. In practice a good QA engineer uses grey-box knowledge to write tests that cover both happy paths and risky internal branches.
questions.realTimeExample: While testing a banking fund-transfer API, I used black-box tests to check that a valid transfer returns a success response, and grey-box knowledge of the ledger tables to verify the debit and credit rows were actually written correctly. The developers used white-box unit tests to cover the interest-calculation branches.

questions.question: What are the types of black-box testing?
questions.answer: Black-box testing is divided into functional and non-functional categories. Functional black-box types include unit, integration, system, smoke, sanity, regression, retesting, acceptance (alpha, beta, UAT) and exploratory or ad-hoc testing. Non-functional black-box types include performance, load, stress, usability, accessibility, security and compatibility testing. Under functional black-box testing come classic test-design techniques such as equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables, state transition testing, use case testing, pairwise (all-pairs) testing and error guessing. All of these rely purely on inputs, outputs and specifications rather than code inspection. Interviewers often expect you to name the design techniques, not just the test levels, because the techniques are what you actually use to derive test cases.
questions.realTimeExample: For a loan-eligibility calculator with an age field, I applied boundary value analysis to test ages 17, 18, 60 and 61, equivalence partitioning to group valid and invalid ranges, and decision-table testing to combine age, income and credit-score rules - all without ever looking at the source code.

questions.question: What is functional testing, and how does it differ from non-functional testing? Give examples.
questions.answer: Functional testing verifies what the system does - it checks each feature against its requirements by feeding inputs and verifying outputs, without judging how well it performs. Non-functional testing verifies how well the system behaves in terms of performance, security, usability, reliability, scalability and compatibility. Functional testing answers 'does the login reject an invalid password?', while non-functional testing answers 'how many users can log in per second before the response time degrades?'. Functional tests are usually pass/fail against expected business behaviour, whereas non-functional tests are measured against thresholds such as response time under 2 seconds or zero critical vulnerabilities. Both are essential: a feature can work correctly yet still be too slow or insecure to ship.
questions.realTimeExample: On a ticketing website, functional testing confirmed that selecting seats and paying produced a valid booking. Non-functional testing confirmed the site could handle 10,000 concurrent users on a concert launch day and that the payment page was served over HTTPS with no exposed card data.

questions.question: What is system testing?
questions.answer: System testing is end-to-end testing of the complete, integrated application to verify that it satisfies the specified requirements as a whole. It is performed after integration testing, on a fully assembled build in an environment that closely resembles production, and it treats the system as a black box. It covers both functional and non-functional aspects - user flows, data integrity, performance, security and usability - and is usually driven by testers rather than developers. System testing is the last level before acceptance testing and aims to catch issues that only surface when all components work together. Exit criteria usually include a target defect closure rate and no blocking or critical defects open.
questions.realTimeExample: Before an airline booking app release, system testing took a complete journey: search a flight, select seats, add baggage, apply a promo code, pay, and receive a confirmation email - all in a production-like staging environment with a real database and payment sandbox.

questions.question: What is integration testing? Give an example and explain how you verify it in your project.
questions.answer: Integration testing verifies that individually working modules interact correctly when combined, focusing on interfaces, data flow and message passing between components. It is performed after unit testing and before system testing, using approaches such as big-bang, top-down, bottom-up or sandwich (hybrid). The goal is to expose defects in the glue between modules - wrong field mappings, mismatched data types, incorrect API contracts, or timing and transaction issues. In a project I verify it by identifying the integration points (UI to API, API to database, service to service, application to payment gateway), then writing scenario tests that exercise real data through those interfaces. Where possible I use stubs or mocks for external systems that are not ready, and I check both the response returned and any side effects such as database writes.
questions.realTimeExample: On an e-commerce project I tested the Order service calling the Payment service: after placing an order I verified the payment gateway was charged, the order status changed to CONFIRMED, and a row was written to the payments table - a classic integration check across three components that worked perfectly alone.

questions.question: Is unit testing done by the developer or the tester?
questions.answer: Unit testing is normally performed by developers, because it requires knowledge of the internal code and is written alongside the source using frameworks such as JUnit, NUnit, pytest or Jest. It tests the smallest testable pieces - methods, functions or classes - in isolation, usually with mocks for dependencies. Testers may occasionally contribute when they have automation or white-box skills, but their primary responsibility lies at integration, system and acceptance levels. In Agile teams the boundary is collaborative: developers unit-test their own code and testers focus on behaviour, edge cases and integration, providing feedback on coverage. Many teams enforce unit tests in the CI pipeline and measure coverage so that a build fails if critical units are untested.
questions.realTimeExample: On a payments team the developer wrote a unit test proving the fee-calculator returned the correct amount for zero, one and many transactions. I, as the tester, never wrote that unit test but reviewed the coverage report and instead tested the calculator's behaviour through the checkout UI.

questions.question: What is the difference between smoke, sanity and regression testing?
questions.answer: Smoke testing is a shallow, broad check that the build is stable enough to test - it verifies that critical features open and basic flows work, and is done on every new build. Sanity testing is a narrow, deep check of a specific area after a small change or fix, confirming that the change works and did not obviously break that module. Regression testing is a broad, deep re-execution of existing test cases to make sure that changes have not broken previously working functionality. Smoke is about build acceptance, sanity is about focused verification of a change, and regression is about protecting existing behaviour. In terms of scope and depth: smoke is wide but shallow, sanity is narrow but deep, and regression is wide and deep, usually automated.
questions.realTimeExample: After the nightly build, I ran a 15-minute smoke suite (login, search, add to cart, checkout) before anything else. When a developer fixed the coupon bug, I ran a sanity test on the coupon screen, and before the release I ran the full automated regression suite of 300 cases.

questions.question: What is the difference between retesting and regression testing?
questions.answer: Retesting (also called confirmation testing) is the re-execution of the specific failed test cases after a defect has been fixed, to confirm the bug is actually gone. Regression testing is a wider activity that re-runs existing tests around a change to ensure the fix or feature did not break anything else that used to work. Retesting is defect-driven, targeted and often manual; regression is change-driven, broad and usually automated. Retesting proves the fix works, while regression proves nothing else broke as a side effect. They are complementary: you retest the exact defect and then run regression on the impacted areas before closing the ticket.
questions.realTimeExample: When our developer fixed a bug where an expired coupon was still accepted, I retested that exact scenario to confirm the fix. Because the coupon code was shared with the cart and order modules, I also ran regression tests on cart totals and order pricing to make sure the change had not broken them.
questions.code:
# Retest the single fixed defect case
mvn test -Dtest=CouponTest#applyExpiredCoupon_isRejected

# Then run the broader impacted regression suite
mvn test -Dgroups=regression -Dtest.impacted=cart,orders

questions.question: When a build arrives, which do you perform first - smoke, sanity, regression or retesting?
questions.answer: The very first thing you do on a new build is smoke testing, to confirm the build is deployable and the critical paths are not broken. If smoke passes, you proceed with sanity testing on the specific change or module the build was meant to fix, and then retesting of the exact defect cases if a fix was included. Only after those pass do you run the full regression suite to confirm existing functionality is unaffected. The logic is to fail fast: there is no point running a heavy regression suite on a build that cannot even log in. So the order is smoke, then sanity and retesting, then regression, all followed by a short report to the team.
questions.realTimeExample: Every morning our CI produced a fresh build. I first ran the smoke suite, and when it failed at login I rejected the build immediately and told the team, saving hours that would otherwise have been wasted on regression against a broken build.

questions.question: What is the difference between alpha and beta testing?
questions.answer: Alpha testing is performed at the developer's site by internal employees or a dedicated QA team before the product is released to external users, and it is often done in a controlled, near-lab environment. Beta testing is performed by real external users at their own locations using the near-final product, providing real-world feedback before general availability. Alpha testing focuses on internal acceptance and catching major issues, while beta testing validates the product under genuine usage conditions, networks and devices. Alpha is controlled and closed, beta is uncontrolled and more open, and both are forms of acceptance testing. Beta feedback is valuable for usability and environment-specific issues that internal testing rarely uncovers.
questions.realTimeExample: For a fitness-tracking app, alpha testing was done by our own employees on a staging build to confirm core features were stable, and then beta testing shipped the app to 500 volunteer users who reported crashing on specific older Android devices.

questions.question: What is utility testing, and is it considered functional testing?
questions.answer: Utility testing checks the supporting, non-core aspects of an application - for example accessibility, usability, error handling, help and documentation, installability, offline behaviour, and whether the product provides value and is easy to use. It is generally classified as non-functional testing because it evaluates qualities of the system rather than verifying a specific business requirement against expected output. It can indirectly support functional expectations (for example, a clear error message on a failed transaction), but its core focus is the quality attribute, not the computed result. Some teams treat utility testing as part of usability or quality-in-use testing. In an interview, the safest answer is that it is primarily non-functional, while acknowledging it can overlap with functional checks around messaging and recovery.
questions.realTimeExample: On a banking app we ran utility testing to confirm the help section explained fee charges clearly, error messages were actionable when a transfer failed, and the app worked offline for balance viewing - none of which verified a calculation but all influenced user trust.

questions.question: How do you approach exploratory testing? Give an example where it found a defect.
questions.answer: Exploratory testing is simultaneous learning, test design and execution, where the tester uses skill, experience and curiosity rather than pre-written scripts. I approach it with time-boxed session-based testing using a charter that states the mission, the area under test and the risks to probe, and I record what I tried and what I found. I start with the critical user journeys, then deliberately push boundaries - unusual inputs, interrupted workflows, back-button and refresh behaviour, and combinations the scripted cases missed. I take notes and screenshots so the findings are reproducible and can be turned into proper test cases. Exploratory testing complements scripted regression by finding defects that structured cases never anticipate.
questions.realTimeExample: While exploring a hotel-booking site, I had a booking open, refreshed the browser mid-payment, and the page re-submitted the charge, creating a duplicate reservation. That defect was never covered by a scripted test case and was fixed by adding a payment idempotency token.

questions.question: How do you perform browser-compatibility testing, and what non-functional testing is required?
questions.answer: Browser-compatibility testing checks that the application renders and behaves consistently across browsers, versions, operating systems, screen sizes and devices. I first analyse the analytics and requirement documents to build a supported matrix of the most-used combinations, then test the critical flows on high-priority browsers and smoke-check the rest. I use real devices where possible and tools such as BrowserStack or Sauce Labs for coverage, and I compare layout, functionality, JavaScript behaviour and network responses. This is fundamentally non-functional testing because it evaluates the quality attribute of compatibility rather than a business requirement. Related non-functional testing that often accompanies it includes usability, accessibility (WCAG), responsive design and performance across those environments.
questions.realTimeExample: For a retail site we prioritised Chrome, Safari and Edge plus iOS Safari and Android Chrome based on analytics. Testing revealed the date picker failed to open on older Safari versions, which we only caught because Safari was on our supported matrix.

questions.question: What is the difference between a defect (bug), an error and a failure?
questions.answer: An error is a human mistake made during requirements, design or coding - for example a developer typing the wrong comparison operator. A defect (or bug) is the flaw in the software that results from that error and is found during testing before release. A failure is the observable deviation from expected behaviour that occurs when the defective code is executed by a user or test. In short: error is the cause, defect is the fault in the code, and failure is the symptom in behaviour. A single defect can cause many failures, and a defect may exist in code that is never exercised, so it never produces a visible failure. Testers find defects during testing and failures during execution, and both are recorded for the developer to fix the underlying error.
questions.realTimeExample: A developer mistakenly wrote 'if (age > 18)' instead of '>= 18' - that is the error. The resulting defect is in the eligibility code. It showed up as a failure when a user who was exactly 18 was wrongly rejected by the loan application.

questions.question: What is the test pyramid?
questions.answer: The test pyramid is a model that recommends having many fast, cheap, low-level tests and progressively fewer slow, expensive, high-level tests. The base is unit tests (the most numerous), the middle is integration or service tests, and the narrow top is UI or end-to-end tests (the fewest). The rationale is speed, cost and reliability: unit tests run in milliseconds and pinpoint failures, while end-to-end tests are slow and flaky and only confirm broad behaviour. An inverted pyramid - too many UI tests - leads to slow, brittle suites that teams stop trusting. The model guides automation strategy so that most logic is covered cheaply at the bottom and only critical journeys are covered end-to-end at the top.
questions.realTimeExample: On a checkout service we had roughly 800 unit tests, 120 API/integration tests and 15 critical end-to-end UI tests through checkout. A pricing bug was caught in seconds by a unit test, while only our money-path journey lived at the expensive UI level.

questions.question: What are test metrics, and how do they relate to TDD and test management?
questions.answer: Test metrics are quantitative measures used to understand and manage testing - examples include test case pass and fail rates, defect density, defect leakage to production, defect rejection ratio, test execution progress, automation coverage, code coverage and mean time to detect or fix. They help a test manager make decisions about release readiness, resource allocation, quality trends and where to invest automation. They relate strongly to TDD (Test-Driven Development), where code coverage and test-first granularity are core metrics that show how much behaviour is protected by unit tests. Good metrics drive action rather than vanity: for instance a rising defect-leakage rate signals gaps in regression, and low coverage in TDD signals risky modules. Managers combine execution metrics with quality metrics to report status honestly to stakeholders.
questions.realTimeExample: In a release review our dashboard showed 95 percent execution, 3 open high defects and 2 percent production leakage. That leakage trend told the manager our regression suite missed a module, so we added automated tests there before approving the next release.

questions.question: What is risk-based testing, and how do you perform it?
questions.answer: Risk-based testing prioritises test effort according to the likelihood and impact of failure, so that the highest-risk areas are tested first and most deeply. I start by identifying risks with the team, usually in a workshop, and score each one by probability times impact (for example high/medium/low), producing a risk register. Then I allocate more test cases, earlier execution and deeper coverage to high-risk items, and lighter coverage to low-risk ones. Risk can come from complex logic, frequent change, business criticality, integration points and areas with past defects. This approach is essential when time is limited because it ensures the most damaging failures are caught before release. I also re-rank risks as the project progresses and new information emerges.
questions.realTimeExample: For a tax-filing platform, the calculation engine and payment submission were scored critical, while the FAQ page was low. With two weeks left we tested the engine exhaustively and gave the FAQ a quick smoke check, catching a rounding defect that would have mis-stated thousands of returns.

questions.question: Explain root-cause-analysis techniques.
questions.answer: Root cause analysis (RCA) is the structured process of finding the underlying reason a defect occurred so it can be prevented, not just fixed. Common techniques include the 5 Whys (repeatedly asking why until the true cause is exposed), fishbone or Ishikawa diagrams (grouping causes into categories such as people, process, tools, environment and requirements), Pareto analysis (focusing on the few causes responsible for most defects) and fault tree analysis for complex failure chains. A simple, effective approach is to reproduce the defect, examine the code and logs, trace it back through design and requirements, and identify the earliest point where it could have been caught. The output is a corrective and preventive action - for example adding a missing test case, a linting rule or a review gate. RCA also feeds metrics like defect leakage so recurring causes become visible over time.
questions.realTimeExample: A checkout bug shipped because two developers merged conflicting coupon rules. Using the 5 Whys we traced it to a missing review on the pricing module, and the preventive action was adding a mandatory code-review rule and an automated pricing regression test before merge.

questions.question: What are the do's and don'ts for a tester?
questions.answer: Do's: understand the requirements before writing tests, design cases for both positive and negative scenarios, test early and continuously, log clear and reproducible defects with evidence, keep tests independent and maintainable, communicate risks honestly, and think like an end user while staying curious. Don'ts: never assume a feature works without verifying it, never log vague or duplicate defects, never test only the happy path, never hide a defect or delay reporting it, avoid blaming developers, and never mark work complete without properly executed evidence. A tester should also avoid destructive changes to shared environments and should keep test data and credentials secure. Ultimately a good tester is thorough, objective, detail-oriented and a strong communicator.
questions.realTimeExample: When I found that a password-reset link never expired, I reproduced it three times, attached a screen recording and steps to the Jira ticket, and flagged it as high security risk. I did not silently fix it or hide it, and I informed the security lead immediately.

questions.question: What is the difference between a test scenario and a test case?
questions.answer: A test scenario is a high-level one-line statement of what needs to be verified, usually derived directly from a requirement, for example 'Verify login with valid and invalid credentials'. A test case is the detailed procedure that proves that scenario, containing a unique ID, preconditions, test data, exact steps, the expected result and postconditions. One scenario normally expands into many test cases covering positive, negative, boundary and edge conditions. Scenarios help you estimate scope and get quick stakeholder sign-off, while test cases drive execution, give repeatability and form the basis for traceability and automation. In practice a senior tester or test lead writes scenarios and any team member can write and execute the cases. In short, the scenario answers 'what to test' and the test case answers 'how to test it, with which data, and what result is expected'.
questions.realTimeExample: On an e-commerce checkout the scenario might be 'Verify the discount coupon applied during checkout'. That single scenario expands into test cases for a valid coupon, an expired coupon, a coupon below the minimum order value, a coupon stacked with another offer, and the same coupon used twice.

questions.question: What points (give five) do you consider when writing a good test case?
questions.answer: Five things I always enforce are: a clear, unique and descriptive title or ID; explicit preconditions and the exact test data needed; numbered, atomic steps that a new tester could follow without guessing; one unambiguous expected result per case that states the exact output, message or state; and a link back to the requirement or user story so coverage is traceable. On top of those I keep each case focused on one objective, make it independent so it can run in any order, keep it reusable for regression, and avoid hard-coding environment-specific values. A good test case is also reviewable, meaning a peer can validate it before execution, and it should state any postconditions or cleanup needed. If a case cannot be executed the same way by two different people, it is not written well enough.
questions.realTimeExample: For a banking app transfer, a good case says: precondition 'user has 2 active accounts', data 'balance 5000 in savings', steps 'open Transfer, select accounts, enter 1000, submit', expected 'success message and savings balance becomes 4000'. That leaves no room for interpretation when another tester runs it during regression.

questions.question: What is test design? Explain the test design techniques you use to create efficient test cases.
questions.answer: Test design is the activity of turning requirements and risks into a structured, minimum-but-sufficient set of test conditions and cases that will find defects efficiently. I select techniques based on the input type: equivalence partitioning to collapse huge input ranges into representative classes, boundary value analysis to test the edges where off-by-one bugs live, and decision tables when business rules combine multiple conditions such as eligibility and fee waivers. For workflows with states I use state transition testing, and for features with many independent parameters I use pairwise or combinatorial testing to drastically reduce the combination count while keeping good defect-detection power. I round this out with experience-based techniques such as error guessing and checklist-based testing from past defect patterns, and use-case or scenario testing for end-to-end journeys. The goal is maximum coverage and defect yield for the least number of cases, so I always justify why a chosen set is sufficient.
questions.realTimeExample: For an insurance premium calculator with age bands, vehicle type, region and no-claim years, brute force would be hundreds of cases. I use equivalence partitioning and boundary values on age and no-claim years, then pairwise combinations of the remaining fields, cutting execution to a couple of dozen high-yield cases.

questions.question: What is your process for creating test cases for a new feature and updating them during development?
questions.answer: I start by reading the requirement, user story and its acceptance criteria, then hold a quick clarification session with the BA or developer to close ambiguities before writing anything. I identify test conditions using the right design techniques, write scenarios first for scope agreement, then expand them into detailed cases with data and expected results, and get a peer or developer to review them early. During development I keep them in the test management tool linked to the story, and I update them when acceptance criteria change or when refining clarifies behaviour. When the build is ready I execute them, and any deviation between expected and actual triggers either a defect or a case update if the spec genuinely changed. After the feature is done I move the stable cases into the regression suite and retire duplicate or obsolete ones so the suite stays lean. I treat test cases as living artefacts, version-controlled through the tool, not a one-time document.
questions.realTimeExample: While a 'save card for faster checkout' feature was being built, the acceptance criteria changed so the card is never saved for guest users. I updated those cases, added a new negative case, re-ran the affected set and kept the rest of the suite intact.

questions.question: What is a test plan, and what does it include?
questions.answer: A test plan is a document that defines how testing for a specific project or release will be organised, executed and controlled. It typically includes the objectives and scope (what is in and out of scope), the test approach and types of testing, test items and features to be tested, entry and exit criteria, the test environment and required test data, roles and responsibilities, the schedule and milestones, and the deliverables. It also lists assumptions, dependencies, risks with mitigation, the tools to be used, and how defects and results will be reported. The plan is usually written once early and then reviewed and updated as scope changes, and it acts as the agreement between QA and stakeholders. A good plan is concise and actionable rather than a long document nobody reads, and it maps directly to the exit criteria used to decide when testing is done.
questions.realTimeExample: For a mobile banking app release we listed scope as login, transfers and statements, out of scope as the legacy admin portal, defined exit criteria of zero open critical defects and 95 percent pass rate, and named the staging environment and test accounts to be used.

questions.question: What is the difference between a test plan and a test strategy?
questions.answer: A test strategy is a high-level, long-lived document owned by QA leadership that defines the organisation's overall testing philosophy, standards, levels and types of testing, tooling, entry and exit norms and reporting conventions across all projects. A test plan is project or release specific, shorter-lived, and derives from the strategy to describe how that particular effort will be executed, scheduled and measured. The strategy answers 'how do we test here in general', while the plan answers 'how will we test this release, with whom, when and against which criteria'. There is normally one strategy per organisation or product line and one plan per project or release. A plan must stay compliant with the strategy, but it can tailor scope, risks and schedules to the specific feature. In interviews the key point is that strategy is broad and stable, plan is narrow and time-bound.
questions.realTimeExample: Our company strategy mandates risk-based testing, Jira with Xray and automation of smoke suites. The plan for the 'instant loan' release then specifies which risk-based areas to prioritise, the exact sprint schedule and the 40 percent automation target for that release.

questions.question: What is a traceability matrix, and how is it used?
questions.answer: A traceability matrix (RTM) is a table that maps requirements or user stories to their test cases, and often also to defects, so you can prove every requirement is covered and every test exists for a reason. It is built by listing requirement IDs down one axis and test case IDs across the other, marking which cases satisfy which requirement, and tracking the pass or fail status. Its main uses are coverage verification, impact analysis when a requirement changes, and evidence for audits or regulated projects. It also exposes gaps, such as a requirement with no test case, and orphan tests that no longer map to any requirement. In an agile tool like Jira with Xray the matrix is generated automatically from issue links rather than maintained by hand. I update it whenever requirements or test cases change so it always reflects reality.
questions.realTimeExample: Before a healthcare app audit we produced an RTM showing each HIPAA-related requirement mapped to its cases and results. It immediately revealed that two encryption requirements had no test cases, which we filled before the compliance review.
questions.code:
Requirement ID | Requirement              | Test Case IDs   | Status
REQ-101        | Login with OTP           | TC-001, TC-002  | Pass
REQ-102        | Reset password link      | TC-003, TC-004  | Fail
REQ-103        | Account lockout, 3 tries | TC-005          | Not Run

questions.question: How do you ensure a requirement is fully testable?
questions.answer: I check that the requirement is unambiguous, complete, consistent, verifiable and has clear acceptance criteria, ideally in Given-When-Then form, because a requirement I cannot verify is a requirement I cannot test. In practice I look for a defined input, a defined behaviour and a measurable expected outcome, and I flag vague words such as 'fast', 'user-friendly' or 'as needed' because they are not verifiable. If something is missing I raise it in refinement or backlog grooming and ask the BA or product owner for clarification, proposing concrete values such as a response time under two seconds. I also check that the requirement does not contradict another requirement or a business rule, and that boundary and error behaviour are defined. Only after the acceptance criteria are concrete do I treat the story as ready to have test cases designed. This 'testability review' in the three amigos session catches ambiguities before coding starts, which is far cheaper than after.
questions.realTimeExample: A story said 'the search should be fast'. I asked for a number and edge behaviour; it became 'results return within 2 seconds for up to 10,000 records, and an empty state message appears for no matches'. That single clarification made the story testable and non-ambiguous.

questions.question: How do you ensure complete coverage, including all edge cases and negative scenarios for a form?
questions.answer: For a form I work field by field and then across fields: for each field I test valid values, empty or mandatory checks, minimum and maximum length, boundary values just inside and outside the limits, special and unicode characters, leading and trailing spaces, SQL and script injection strings, and format rules such as email or phone patterns. I then add negative scenarios like wrong data types, past dates, invalid file types and oversized uploads, and error-handling checks to confirm the right message appears and no data is silently lost. Cross-field and business-rule cases come next, for example confirm password mismatch, date-of-birth driving an age rule, and conditional fields appearing or hiding based on earlier answers. I also test submission behaviour: disable or duplicate submission, session timeout mid-form, back button, refresh, and re-submitting after a validation failure. Finally I cover accessibility, keyboard and mobile layouts, and I use equivalence partitioning plus boundary analysis so I am systematic rather than randomly exhaustive. This layered approach gives defensible complete coverage without writing thousands of pointless cases.
questions.realTimeExample: On an airline booking passenger form I tested a name with an apostrophe (O'Brien), a 20-character boundary on the passport field, an expired passport date, a mismatched confirm-email, and a double-click on Pay to confirm only one booking was created.

questions.question: How do you decide test coverage when time is limited?
questions.answer: When time is short I switch to risk-based testing: I rank features by business impact, probability of failure, and how recently or heavily they changed, then concentrate the deepest testing on the highest-risk areas. I prioritise the critical user journeys and revenue-impacting flows such as payments and login, run the existing regression smoke suite, and reduce breadth rather than depth on the most sensitive paths. I cover boundaries and negative cases for high-risk fields only, and rely on equivalence partitioning so one representative case stands in for many similar ones. I explicitly document what I am not testing and why, so the risk is visible and signed off by the product owner rather than hidden. I also consider using automation for repetitive regression and shifting some exploratory testing where scripted cases would be too slow. The honest answer I give in interviews is that coverage becomes a deliberate, communicated trade-off, not an accident.
questions.realTimeExample: Two days before a release I skipped cosmetic admin screens and concentrated on the payment flow, coupon logic and login, plus the automated smoke suite. I sent the product owner a one-line note listing the untested admin screens for explicit sign-off.

questions.question: How do you decide when to stop testing a feature?
questions.answer: I stop when the agreed exit criteria are met, not when I feel done: typically all planned cases executed, pass rate at or above target, zero open critical or blocker defects, a declining trend in new defect discovery rate, and required coverage or traceability satisfied. I also watch the defect find rate curve, because when new tests stop finding new defects and the curve flattens, additional testing has diminishing returns. I confirm that high-risk areas and the regression smoke suite are green and that automation is stable. Finally, stopping is a joint decision with the product owner and delivery lead, based on residual risk versus schedule, and I record what is deferred so it is transparent. The exit criteria are defined up front in the test plan precisely so this decision is objective rather than emotional. If criteria are not met but the business decides to ship, I make the residual risk explicit in writing.
questions.realTimeExample: Before shipping a rewards feature, defect discovery dropped from nine per day to one in three days, all exit criteria were green, and the product owner accepted two low-severity cosmetic defects as deferred with a fix scheduled for the next patch.

questions.question: Where do you write and manage test cases (Excel or a tool), and how do you keep documentation in order?
questions.answer: I prefer a dedicated test management tool such as Xray, Zephyr, TestRail or Azure Test Plans because it links cases to user stories and defects, tracks execution history, supports shared steps and generates traceability automatically; Excel only makes sense for very small teams or ad-hoc checklists where there is no tooling budget. I keep documentation in order by using a strict naming convention and unique IDs, grouping cases by feature or module in folders or test sets, keeping a single source of truth so no duplicate copies float around, and versioning changes with the tool rather than saving files like 'v2 final'. I archive obsolete cases instead of deleting them, so history is preserved for audits. I also keep a clear folder for reusable shared steps and a separate regression suite so execution sets stay manageable. Above all, I make sure the cases stay updated with each release, because stale documentation is worse than none.
questions.realTimeExample: On a payments team we kept all cases in Xray linked to Jira stories, grouped into test sets per release and a golden regression set. When someone tried to keep a parallel Excel tracker, we removed it to avoid two sources of truth.

questions.question: What is the X-ray tool, and how is it used?
questions.answer: Xray is a test management application that runs inside Jira and models testing with native issues: Test, Precondition, Test Set, Test Plan, Test Execution and Test Repository. Testers write manual steps with expected results on the Test issue, link Tests to requirements or user stories to build coverage, then group them into Test Sets and include them in Test Plans and Test Executions. Execution records pass or fail status, evidence and defects directly inside Jira, which gives real-time coverage reports, traceability matrices and requirement coverage charts without a separate system. It also integrates with automation through frameworks such as Cucumber, JUnit, Robot and Playwright, where automated results are pushed back as Test Execution items using APIs or CI plugins. In practice it lets QA and developers work in one tool, so status is visible to the whole team on the story itself. The main interview point is that Xray turns Jira into an end-to-end test management system rather than using a disconnected spreadsheet.
questions.realTimeExample: On a Jira project I linked each Checkout user story to Xray Test issues, grouped them in a 'Checkout Regression' Test Set, ran them in a Test Execution per sprint, and raised defects straight from a failed step so the story showed live pass and fail status.

project = PAY AND issuetype = Test AND "Test Set" = "Checkout Regression" AND status != Done

# Xray links Tests to requirements via Test Coverage
# Automation results are imported to a Test Execution via REST API or CI plugin

questions.question: Which test-management and bug-tracking tools do you use?
questions.answer: For bug tracking the industry standard is Jira, with alternatives like Azure DevOps Boards, Bugzilla, Mantis and Rally depending on the organisation. For test management I use Xray or Zephyr when the team is already on Jira, TestRail or qTest when a standalone tool is preferred, and Azure Test Plans when in the Microsoft ecosystem. I complement these with browser developer tools, Postman, Charles or Fiddler for API and traffic inspection, Selenium, Playwright or Cypress for automation, and Git with a CI tool such as Jenkins, GitHub Actions or GitLab CI to run pipelines. Test data and reporting often use SQL clients and dashboards, and lightweight evidence capture uses Snip and Sketch or built-in screenshot tools. The exact stack matters less than being able to explain why each tool is picked and how they work together. In an interview I always tie the tools back to the workflow: design in the management tool, log defects in the tracker, automate in code, execute in CI, and report coverage from linked data.
questions.realTimeExample: In my last project the stack was Jira with Xray for cases and defects, Postman and RestAssured for APIs, Playwright for UI automation, and GitHub Actions to run the nightly regression and push results back into Xray.

questions.question: Explain the bug/defect life cycle with a real example. What does the "Deferred" status mean, and how do you manage defects at an early stage?
questions.answer: The defect life cycle is New (raised by QA), Assigned (routed to a developer), Open/In Progress (developer investigating and fixing), Fixed (code change committed), Ready for Retest, Verified (QA confirms the fix), and Closed; along the way a defect can also go to Rejected, Duplicate, Not a Bug, Cannot Reproduce or Deferred. In a real example I log a wrong-total defect, it is assigned to a developer who fixes it, I retest on the new build and verify the correct total, then close it. 'Deferred' means the defect is valid and accepted but the team has agreed not to fix it in the current release, usually because it is low severity or low priority, and it is carried into the backlog for a future release with a documented reason. At an early stage, when many defects are found, I triage them promptly with the developer and BA to remove duplicates and non-bugs, assign severity and priority, and keep the list short and accurate so real issues are not buried. I always record the deferral decision with who approved it, so if the issue later causes problems there is a clear audit trail.
questions.realTimeExample: On a retail app a minor misalignment in the order-history table was valid but cosmetic, so we marked it Deferred with the product owner's approval and a ticket in the next sprint, while a wrong-tax defect was fixed immediately due to revenue impact.

questions.question: What is the difference between severity and priority? Who decides each, can they change, and give examples such as high priority/low severity and high severity/low priority.
questions.answer: Severity is the technical impact of a defect on the system, how badly functionality or data is broken, and it is normally decided by QA or the tester who found it. Priority is the business urgency of fixing it, how soon it must be addressed relative to other work, and it is decided by the product owner or business in agreement with the delivery lead. Severity can change as investigation reveals more impact, and priority changes as business conditions change, for example a missing feature becomes urgent once a launch date moves. They are independent axes: a high-severity but low-priority example is a crash that only occurs in a rarely used legacy report used once a year; a low-severity but high-priority example is a typo in the company name on the homepage or a wrong logo on the invoice, which does not break anything technically but damages credibility immediately. The classic mismatch examples are the ones interviewers expect, so I always give both. Severity and priority combined drive the order in which defects are fixed and released.
questions.realTimeExample: A broken 'print invoice' option that only affects an unused paper format was high severity, low priority. A misspelled brand name on the login screen was low severity, high priority because marketing wanted it fixed before a campaign launch.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Blocker and a Critical bug?
questions.answer: A Blocker is a defect that stops testing or development from proceeding at all, for example the application will not start, the login fails for everyone, or the environment is down, so there is no workaround and the flow cannot continue. A Critical defect is a severe functional failure with major business impact, such as a payment being charged twice or data corruption, but testing of other areas can often still proceed and there may rarely be a workaround. In short, Blocker is about 'I cannot continue testing' and Critical is about 'the product is badly broken for the user'. Both are typically fixed immediately, but the classification matters because a blocker halts the whole team and is escalated instantly, while a critical defect is prioritised as top severity within the normal fix queue. Priority is almost always highest for both, but severity of a blocker is context-dependent, since a broken test environment has huge testing impact yet no end-user impact. I report blockers with an immediate call or message as well as a ticket, rather than waiting for triage.
questions.realTimeExample: When the staging build would not launch after a deployment, that was a Blocker escalated at once. Separately, a defect that applied the discount twice and overcharged customers was Critical, high severity and high priority, but the rest of regression could still run.

questions.question: What should a good bug report contain, and what steps do you follow to log a defect in Jira?
questions.answer: A good bug report has a clear and specific summary, the exact environment and build, preconditions, numbered steps to reproduce, the expected result, the actual result, the severity and priority, and supporting evidence such as screenshots, logs, trace or HAR files and a status of reproducibility. In Jira I first search for an existing ticket to avoid duplicates, then create a Bug issue in the correct project with the right component and labels, fill the summary and the description with the structured fields above, attach evidence, set severity and priority, link the related story or test case, and assign it to the right team or leave it for triage. I then confirm the ticket appears in the board and follow up on it until it is triaged. The two rules I never break are one defect per ticket and reproducible steps, because vague reports waste developer time and get bounced back. A report is only good if someone else can reproduce the issue without asking me a single question.
questions.realTimeExample: For a checkout defect I raised: 'Order total shows 0.00 when a 100 percent coupon is applied', attached the console log and a screenshot, set severity Critical and priority High, and linked it to the Checkout story and the failing test case.
questions.code:
Summary: [Checkout] Order total shows 0.00 when 100 percent coupon applied
Environment: Staging / Chrome 125 / build 4.2.1
Preconditions: User logged in, 2 items in cart
Steps: 1) Add 2 items  2) Apply coupon FREESHIP100  3) Click Pay
Expected: Total equals shipping fee, payment page opens
Actual: Total shows 0.00 and Pay button is disabled
Severity: Critical   Priority: High
Attachments: screenshot, console log, HAR file

questions.question: What is bug/defect leakage, how do you calculate it, and how do you handle it?
questions.answer: Defect leakage, sometimes called escaped defects, measures how many defects were not caught during testing and were found later by users or in production, which directly indicates how effective the testing was. It is commonly calculated as defects found in production divided by the total of production defects plus defects found in testing, expressed as a percentage, and there is a related 'defect removal efficiency' metric which is the inverse. When leakage is high I do a root-cause analysis rather than blame: was the requirement ambiguous, was the case missing, was the test environment different from production, was the change untested in regression, or did a hotfix bypass QA? I then act on that cause, for example adding the missing cases, improving test data, strengthening the regression suite or automating the gap, and I track whether leakage trends down over subsequent releases. I also share the metric in retrospectives because leakage is a team learning signal, not an individual performance number. The goal is a measurable, sustained reduction, not a one-off explanation.
questions.realTimeExample: After a release, users in production reported that saved cards were not appearing on some Android devices. The gap was that device coverage only included iOS, so we added two Android models to the device lab and the corresponding cases, and leakage dropped the following sprint.
questions.code:
Defect Leakage % = (Defects found in Production / (Defects found in Production + Defects found in Testing)) * 100

Example:
  Production defects = 6
  Testing defects    = 94
  Defect Leakage %   = 6 / (6 + 94) * 100 = 6 %

questions.question: You find three related bugs. Do you report them separately or combine them?
questions.answer: It depends on whether they share one root cause and one fix, because the guiding principle is one defect per ticket so tracking, severity and fixes stay clean. If all three are symptoms of the same underlying issue, for example three fields all accepting the wrong date format because one shared validation component is broken, I log a single defect that lists the affected fields as evidence, which avoids duplicate fixes and keeps the fix small. If they are related by feature but have different root causes, different severities, or could be fixed and released independently, I log them as separate defects and link them as 'relates to' so the team sees the cluster. I must never bundle unrelated issues into one ticket, because then part-fixes make status ambiguous and the ticket can never be closed cleanly. Practically I first investigate to identify whether the cause is common, then decide, and I always tell the developer in the ticket that the others are linked. This keeps the defect list accurate and the fix verifiable.
questions.realTimeExample: In a checkout form, the phone, ZIP and card fields all accepted letters because one regex was wrong, so I raised a single defect listing all three. But a separate rounding error on tax was a different cause, so it got its own linked ticket.

questions.question: A developer rejects your bug as "not a bug / works as designed". How do you justify it?
questions.answer: First I stay objective and assume good intent, because a rejection is usually a requirements misunderstanding rather than a dispute. I re-read the acceptance criteria, user story, design or spec and gather my evidence: the exact steps, the actual versus expected result, screenshots, logs and, where useful, a short video of the reproduction. Then I reopen the conversation in the ticket or a quick call, present the evidence calmly and ask the developer or BA to point to the requirement that says the current behaviour is correct. If the spec genuinely says it works as designed but the behaviour is still wrong or confusing for users, I reframe it as a usability or requirements gap and involve the product owner to make the call. If I am proven wrong I accept it gracefully and update my test case so the correct expected result is documented. The key is to let evidence and requirements decide, not seniority or volume.
questions.realTimeExample: A developer said the app showing an error on an empty search was 'as designed'. I attached the story's acceptance criteria which explicitly required an empty-state message, and the product owner confirmed it, so the ticket was reopened and fixed.

questions.question: Developers mark a bug "Not Reproducible" (or "works on my machine") but you can reproduce it. What do you check and do?
questions.answer: When this happens I first verify I am on the same build, environment, browser version, user role and test data as the developer, since most 'cannot reproduce' cases come from environment or data differences. I then capture the reproduction precisely: a screen recording, exact steps with a session id, the request and response with a HAR file, console or server logs, and the exact timestamp, then attach all of it to the ticket and re-assign with those details. If the developer still cannot reproduce, I check whether it is data-dependent such as a specific user account, cache or cookie dependent, or intermittent by nature. Using a shared session over remote control or a quick paired debugging call often resolves the mismatch in minutes. If the issue is intermittent I retitle the defect to mark it intermittent and include the observed frequency, rather than forcing a binary repro. Throughout I keep it collaborative, because my goal is a fix, not to win the argument.
questions.realTimeExample: A cart defect only appeared for users with an old session cookie. I cleared my cache, reproduced it again, attached the HAR file and cookie state, then shared my screen with the developer, who saw it immediately and fixed a stale-state bug.

questions.question: You cannot reproduce a bug consistently (it appears 1 in 10 times). Do you log it, and how?
questions.answer: Yes, I always log it, because an intermittent defect in a live system is still a real defect and is often the most valuable one to catch before users hit it at scale. I log it clearly as intermittent in the title, record the observed frequency such as roughly one attempt in ten, and include the exact conditions: timestamps, environment, build, user or session id, steps, and any evidence like a screen recording of a failing run and the console or server logs from that moment. I explicitly note that it is timing, load, race-condition or data dependent where I suspect so, and I list what I tried to make it fail more reliably. I set a realistic severity based on the impact if it does occur, because a one-in-ten failure on payment is far more serious than on a cosmetic label. I keep probing to find a trigger, such as concurrent requests, slow network or a specific sequence, and I update the ticket with any pattern I find. If the team decides to defer it, the intermittent evidence and frequency stay on record so it is not forgotten.
questions.realTimeExample: A double-charge happened about once in ten rapid checkout attempts under slow network. I attached an eight-second video of the failing run, the two charge IDs from the logs and the exact timing, then found the cause was a missing idempotency key on a retried request.
questions.code:
Bug ID: BUG-4821
Title: [Intermittent] Cart total wrong when two coupons applied
Frequency: about 1 in 10 attempts (3 of 30 runs)
Environment: Chrome 125 / staging / user id 88213
Suspect: race condition on retried request
Evidence: HAR file, console log, screen recording (00:42), timestamps
Impact: wrong amount charged if the order is placed

questions.question: A developer is not fixing a bug. How do you approach the situation?
questions.answer: I start by understanding why rather than escalating immediately: the developer may disagree on severity, be blocked, be overloaded, or believe the fix is risky, so a short direct conversation usually clarifies it. If it is a prioritisation issue I bring the facts to the sprint review or triage, showing user impact, the number of affected users and the business risk, and let the product owner decide the priority. I make sure the ticket is clean and evidenced so the decision is based on facts, and I keep it visible on the board so it is not lost in a backlog. If it is a low-severity cosmetic issue I accept that it may be legitimately deferred, while if it is high impact I escalate through the test lead or manager with the evidence. I maintain a professional, collaborative tone throughout because the goal is the fix and a good working relationship, not to attribute blame. Whichever way it goes, I always record the decision and its owner on the ticket.
questions.realTimeExample: A developer kept pushing back on a data-export defect. I showed in triage that three enterprise customers had reported it, the product owner raised its priority, and it was fixed in the next sprint instead of drifting through several releases.

questions.question: You disagree with a developer (or the team) about a bug's severity/priority. How do you handle it?
questions.answer: I separate the two things first: severity is technically objective and I justify it with evidence such as error logs, data loss or the number of users affected, but priority is a business judgement that I do not own, so disagreement there is resolved with the product owner. I present my reasoning with concrete impact, for example 'this corrupts saved data and cannot be undone', and I listen genuinely because the developer often has technical context I lack. If we still disagree, we agree to disagree and escalate to the product owner or test lead, whose decision I accept and document, because the team needs a clear owner for the call. I avoid turning it into a personal argument or blocking the release over a classification, since the priority only affects sequencing, not whether the defect is real. I also revisit the severity if new information appears during the fix. The professional outcome is a documented, evidence-based decision that everyone understands.
questions.realTimeExample: A developer rated a session-logout-before-save bug as medium; I showed that users lost unsaved form data, so the product owner agreed to high priority. The severity stayed the same but the fix was pulled forward.

questions.question: A bug exists in Prod but is not reproducible in QA. How do you investigate?
questions.answer: My first assumption is that production differs from QA in data, configuration, version or load, so I investigate those systematically. I confirm the exact build and version deployed to production, since a hotfix or config-only change may not be in QA, and I compare feature flags, environment variables and third-party service versions between environments. Next I look at the data: the specific user, account, locale or record that triggers it, because production data volumes and edge-case records often reveal what clean QA data hides. I pull production logs, traces, APM data, error tracking and the sequence of calls around the timestamp to reconstruct what happened, and I check whether it is load or concurrency related. I then try to reproduce in QA by cloning the relevant production data or configuration, or by reproducing against a production-like read-only environment, and I keep the ticket documented with every hypothesis and result. If it still cannot be reproduced I may use a canary or feature flag and enhanced logging to capture it live, rather than closing it. Throughout I coordinate closely with the developer and ops, because production-only issues are rarely a QA-only problem.
questions.realTimeExample: A discount error appeared for one enterprise customer in production but never in QA. Comparing configs, the customer used a legacy price-list flag not enabled in QA; turning it on in a test environment reproduced the defect immediately.

questions.question: You found a bug that also exists in a lower environment. What do you do?
questions.answer: Finding the same bug in a lower environment is actually useful, because it confirms the defect is systematic rather than environment-specific and gives the developer a faster place to debug and fix it. I check which environments are affected, verify on the exact same build where possible, and record that information in the ticket so the team knows the full impact and can decide where to fix and verify first. If it exists in production as well as QA or staging, I raise the priority because live users are affected, and I flag it explicitly to the product owner rather than leaving it buried. I then verify the fix in the lowest environment first, propagate and confirm it in each higher environment in order, and finally confirm in production after the release. I also assess whether other features or environments share the same root cause, so a single fix covers all instances. The key behaviour is not just logging the duplicate finding but driving it to a verified fix across every affected environment.
questions.realTimeExample: A tax rounding bug I found in QA also existed in staging and production. We raised it to high priority, fixed it once on the shared service, verified in QA, then staging, and confirmed on production after the release.

questions.question: How do you decide which test cases to automate and which to keep manual?
questions.answer: I triage each candidate case against a few practical criteria: it must be stable, repeatable, high-value, and executed often. Automation pays off for smoke/sanity checks, regression suites, data-driven validations, API and integration layers, and anything that runs on every build. I keep cases manual when they need human judgment, exploratory thinking, visual or UX perception, or when they run once and change constantly. I also weigh ROI: if building and maintaining the script costs more than running it manually over its lifetime, it stays manual. The golden rule is to automate the boring but critical and keep humans for the curious and subjective.
questions.realTimeExample: On an e-commerce checkout I automated login, add-to-cart, the payment-gateway happy path, and 40 regression checks because they run every build. I kept the visual polish of the cart badge and the 'feels responsive' checks manual, because a human notices a misaligned button faster than any assertion.

questions.question: Which test cases would you not automate, which features cannot be automated, and is 100% automation possible?
questions.answer: I would not automate tests that rely on subjective judgment such as look-and-feel, usability, and accessibility feel, nor one-off or throwaway checks, exploratory/ad-hoc testing, or cases whose expected result changes every sprint. Features that cannot be reliably automated include CAPTCHA and OTP flows, biometric and hardware interactions, unstable third-party services, physical device peripherals, and some complex visual/canvas rendering. 100% automation is a myth: human validation, exploratory testing, and risk-based judgment can never be fully replaced. A realistic target is roughly 70-85% automation of regression, with manual effort focused where humans add unique value.
questions.realTimeExample: For a banking app we could never automate the SMS OTP reliably, so that step stayed manual or used a test-mode bypass in staging. We automated statement generation and transfers, but a tester still eyeballed colour contrast and error-message wording before each release.

questions.question: What are the benefits of automation testing over manual testing?
questions.answer: Automation runs faster and unattended, giving quick and consistent feedback on every build, including overnight and in CI pipelines. It removes human error and fatigue, so results are repeatable and reliable across environments and data sets. It supports reuse, parallel execution, and wider coverage such as data-driven and cross-browser scenarios that would be impractical to do by hand. Once built, it lowers the long-term cost per execution and frees testers for exploratory and higher-value work. The main trade-off is upfront scripting effort and ongoing maintenance, which must be justified by repetition and stability.
questions.realTimeExample: A nightly Selenium suite ran 600 regression checks for an insurance portal in under an hour, so the team had pass/fail results before standup. Testers then spent the day on new-risk areas and edge cases instead of re-running the same 600 steps manually.

questions.question: If a scenario takes a long time to execute, would you prefer manual or automation testing, and why?
questions.answer: A long-running scenario is usually a strong automation candidate, because automation absorbs the execution time while the tester does something else. If it is stable, repeatable, and needed more than once, I automate it and run it in CI or off-hours. If it is a one-off, setup-heavy, or exploratory scenario, manual may be faster to start but painful to repeat. I would only prefer manual when the scenario needs constant human decisions or the one-time scripting effort clearly outweighs the benefit. Generally, the longer and more repetitive the scenario, the stronger the case for automation.
questions.realTimeExample: A batch end-of-day reconciliation report took 45 minutes to verify manually each release. I scripted it to run overnight, so testers validated the diff report in five minutes the next morning instead of babysitting the run.

questions.question: Do you prefer manual or automation testing, and which is better for the team?
questions.answer: They are complementary, not rivals: I do not have a permanent favourite, I pick the right tool per situation. Automation is better for regression, repetitive, high-volume, and CI-driven checks, while manual is better for exploration, usability, UX, and first-time validation of new features. For a team, the healthiest setup blends both, automating the stable regression backbone and reserving skilled humans for judgment-heavy work. I would recommend automation where it protects release cadence and manual where insight matters more than repetition. The choice is always driven by value and risk, not personal preference.
questions.realTimeExample: On a mobile-banking team I automated the 200-check regression suite but personally explored the new 'freeze card' feature manually, because a tester caught an ambiguous error message that the scripts would have happily passed.

questions.question: How do you pick test cases for regression testing?
questions.answer: I select regression cases using risk and business impact: critical user journeys, high-usage modules, recently changed code, and areas with a history of defects. I include integration points and anything touched by the change, then add a stable core set that always runs as smoke/sanity. I trace the change to requirements and code to find affected areas rather than blindly running everything. Where time is short I prioritise by severity and frequency, and I keep a tagged, re-runnable core suite as the baseline. The selection is dynamic and reviewed as the product evolves, so it never goes stale.
questions.realTimeExample: After a login-module refactor in a retail app, I ran the core smoke set plus every case touching authentication, session handling, and cart persistence, since those depended on the login token. I skipped unrelated CMS content checks that had not changed.

questions.question: How do you perform regression manually and make sure no critical functionality is missed?
questions.answer: I perform manual regression from a maintained regression checklist or suite, executed against clear expected results and prepared test data. I start with smoke/sanity to confirm the build is testable, then run the prioritised core set covering critical functionality first. I use traceability to map changes to affected features so nothing critical is skipped. I record pass/fail with evidence, log defects immediately, and re-test fixed items. Finally I verify the critical paths end-to-end regardless of time pressure, because those are non-negotiable even when other areas get trimmed.
questions.realTimeExample: Before a banking app release I ran a 90-minute manual regression from a prioritised checklist: login, transfers, bill pay, statements, logout. Even under time pressure I always completed the money-movement paths by hand.

questions.question: How do you prioritize test cases - for a large product, and when you have 100 cases with only 3 hours left?
questions.answer: I prioritise by risk and business impact: severity, probability of failure, usage frequency, and revenue or compliance impact. For a large product I tier cases into P0 (critical, always run), P1 (important), and P2 (nice-to-have), and I maintain that mapping continuously. When 100 cases must fit in 3 hours, I run all P0s first, then as many P1s as time allows, and explicitly flag the P2s as deferred with rationale. I may combine or automate repetitive steps to buy time. I always communicate what was not tested so the residual risk is a conscious business decision, not a silent gap.
questions.realTimeExample: Two days before a travel-booking release with 100 cases and 3 hours, I ran the 20 P0 cases (search, book, pay, cancel) first, then 40 P1s. I told the release manager that 40 P2 cosmetic and edge cases were untested so they could accept that risk knowingly.

questions.question: How many test cases have you automated in a single sprint?
questions.answer: There is no fixed number; it depends on complexity, framework maturity, and how much of the sprint is dedicated to automation. On a mature framework with stable features I have automated roughly 20-40 cases in a sprint, but on a new framework or complex flows, 5-10 solid, stable cases is more realistic. I would rather deliver fewer high-quality, maintainable scripts than a large fragile batch that causes false failures. I report automation progress alongside new-feature testing, and I never let a case-count target override quality. Being honest about realistic capacity is more valuable than inflating numbers.
questions.realTimeExample: In one sprint on a mature REST-Assured API framework I automated 32 endpoint and data-validation cases. In the sprint where we first built the framework skeleton I automated only 8, because setup, utilities, and CI wiring consumed most of my time.

questions.question: How do you stop test coverage from rotting as the product evolves?
questions.answer: I treat the suite as a living product with owners, review cycles, and metrics rather than a one-time artifact. I tag and group tests, remove or rewrite flaky and obsolete cases each sprint, and keep a mapping to current requirements so dead tests do not linger. I measure coverage and flakiness and run the suite on every build so drift is caught early. When a feature changes, I update the related tests as part of that sprint's definition of done. Regular pruning and refactoring keep the suite fast, trustworthy, and relevant over time.
questions.realTimeExample: Our web suite grew flaky after several UI redesigns, so we ran a monthly suite-health session: delete tests for removed features, fix the five flakiest scripts, and re-map coverage. Pass reliability rose and the suite stayed fast enough for CI.

questions.question: You inherited a test suite you did not build. What do you do first?
questions.answer: First I do not change anything: I run the suite as-is and record the baseline of passes, failures, and flakiness. I read the framework structure to identify page objects, data handling, config, and CI wiring, and I find out who maintains it. I review a sample of scripts to understand conventions and quality, and I check test reports and known issues. Then I pick one or two quick wins, such as stabilising the flakiest tests or adding reporting, before proposing bigger refactors. This sequence builds trust, avoids breaking what works, and gives me an informed plan instead of guesswork.
questions.realTimeExample: Inheriting a Cypress suite, I first ran it and found 30 of 200 tests flaky. I documented the framework layout, fixed the three worst flaky tests, then proposed a phased cleanup plan to the team rather than rewriting everything on day one.

questions.topic: Test Scenarios & How Would You Test
questions.question: Write test cases for a login page, including negative cases.
questions.answer: A login page is tested by mapping every field, rule and state to positive and negative cases. Start with functional positives: valid credentials log in and land on the correct home page, password is masked, and remember-me persists.
