questions.question: What is the Definition of Done (DoD)?
questions.answer: The Definition of Done is a shared, team-agreed checklist that states exactly what 'complete' means for any work item before it counts as finished. It typically includes code reviewed, unit and integration tests written and passing, automation updated, acceptance criteria met, no open critical defects, documentation updated, and the item demonstrated or deployable. Because it is explicit and owned by the whole team, the DoD prevents 'it works on my machine' arguments and sets a consistent quality bar across stories. It also gives QA a clear gate: a story is not done until every DoD item is genuinely satisfied. I help refine the DoD so testability, automation and relevant non-functional checks are included from the start.
questions.realTimeExample: Our DoD required every story to have peer-reviewed code, passing unit tests, updated regression automation and a QA sign-off on the acceptance criteria. When a developer tried to mark a story done without automation, we held it back until the tests were added, keeping our quality bar consistent release after release.

questions.question: What is velocity in Agile, and how is it calculated?
questions.answer: Velocity is the amount of work a team completes in a sprint, measured in story points rather than hours or ticket counts. It is calculated by summing the points of all fully completed, Definition-of-Done-satisfied stories at the end of each sprint, then averaging those totals over the last few sprints to smooth out noise. Velocity is relative and team-specific, so comparing one team's velocity with another's is meaningless. Its real value is forecasting: if a team averages 30 points per sprint, it can plan roughly that much next sprint and predict delivery dates. Partly completed stories are normally excluded, which nudges the team to finish work rather than start many things at once.
questions.realTimeExample: Our team completed 28, 32 and 30 points over three sprints, giving an average velocity of about 30. When planning the next sprint we used that number as a guide and only committed to around 30 points of work, which kept our commitments realistic and predictable.

questions.question: What estimation techniques do you use, and what is your approach to task estimation?
questions.answer: I use Planning Poker with story points and relative sizing for sprint work, T-shirt sizing (XS to XL) for quick backlog triage, and three-point estimation (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) or Wideband Delphi for larger or uncertain items. My approach is to estimate the whole effort - development, testing and automation - not just coding, and to size tests by complexity and risk rather than counting test cases. I break large stories into smaller ones so estimates fit within a single sprint, and I include buffer for unknowns, data setup and environment effort. I re-estimate when scope changes instead of clinging to an outdated number. Estimation is a team activity, so I openly share test-complexity and data-setup concerns during poker to keep estimates honest.
questions.realTimeExample: During poker for a 'bulk CSV import' story, developers initially estimated 5 points, but I flagged that I needed large, varied test files and negative-case validation, so we agreed on 8. Building that shared understanding up front avoided an unrealistic commitment and a rushed, under-tested delivery.

questions.question: Which metrics do you use to track project progress in Agile?
questions.answer: I track a mix of flow and delivery metrics: a burndown or burnup chart for sprint progress, velocity for capacity forecasting, and a cumulative flow diagram to expose bottlenecks and work-in-progress build-up. I also watch cycle time and lead time to understand how long work really takes end to end, plus throughput for completed items. Quality-oriented metrics such as escaped defects, reopened defects and defect density show whether quality is improving, while a release burndown tracks commitment against delivery. The purpose is to surface problems early and improve predictability, not to game numbers. I review these with the team in retrospectives so they drive real process changes rather than vanity reporting.
questions.realTimeExample: Our cumulative flow diagram showed a growing 'in testing' column mid-sprint, revealing that testing was the bottleneck. We responded by shifting some automation work earlier and adding a mid-sprint test checkpoint, which flattened the flow and improved our on-time completion rate the following sprint.

questions.question: Which KPIs, automation and quality metrics do you monitor, and why?
questions.answer: I monitor KPIs across three areas: test execution, defect health and process flow. Execution metrics include pass/fail rate, automation coverage, suite execution time and flaky-test rate; defect metrics include defect density, escaped defects to production, reopened rate and backlog aging; process metrics include velocity, cycle time and release frequency. Automation metrics matter because they show whether the suite is fast, stable and trusted - a fast but flaky suite is worse than useless. I also track coverage of requirements and acceptance criteria, plus code coverage where available, to expose blind spots. The reason is decision-making: these numbers reveal risk, trend quality over time, justify automation investment and drive targeted improvement. I deliberately focus on a small set of meaningful leading and lagging indicators rather than vanity metrics.
questions.realTimeExample: Our dashboard showed a 96 percent pass rate but a rising flaky-test rate and a climbing count of escaped defects. Rather than celebrate the pass rate, we investigated flakiness first, stabilised the top offenders, and within two sprints escaped defects dropped noticeably because the suite could be trusted again.

questions.question: Your suite has a 98% pass rate but critical bugs still reach production. What could be missing?
questions.answer: A high pass rate only proves the tests you ran passed - it says nothing about tests that were never written or that assert the wrong things. The gap is usually poor coverage and weak test design: happy-path-heavy cases with few negative, edge and integration tests, critical dependencies mocked away, environment drift between test and production, and a regression suite that no longer reflects current behaviour. It can also mean risk analysis and exploratory testing were skipped, so whole risk areas went untested. I would run a root-cause review, map each production defect back to the missing test type, and shift emphasis from pass rate to escaped-defect rate. Then I would strengthen risk-based coverage, add contract and integration tests, and gate releases on meaningful signals rather than a vanity pass percentage.
questions.realTimeExample: A payment service passed 98 percent of tests but broke in production when a third-party gateway returned a slow timeout, because all integration tests mocked that gateway as fast and always successful. We added contract tests and real timeout/error-path cases, and the next release caught the issue in staging instead of production.

questions.question: How would you design an effective quality gate for production deployment?
questions.answer: An effective quality gate is automated, risk-based and blocking: a release proceeds only when clearly defined conditions are met. Typical gates include a green build, unit and integration tests passing with a coverage threshold, the key regression suite green, zero open blocker or critical defects, clean security and static scans, performance thresholds met, and a signed-off release checklist. I encode the gates directly in the CI/CD pipeline so they run consistently on every candidate and fail fast, and I allow an override only through a documented, risk-accepted exception. Gates must be balanced - too strict and teams bypass them, too loose and they are theatre. I set and tune thresholds with the team and revisit them as the product and its risk profile evolve.
questions.realTimeExample: For a banking API we gated production on green build, 80 percent unit coverage, a passing smoke plus critical regression pack, no open P1/P2 and a clean OWASP ZAP scan. When one scan flagged a medium finding, the pipeline blocked deployment until it was fixed, preventing a vulnerable build from shipping.

questions.question: How do you maintain test-execution dashboards?
questions.answer: I maintain test-execution dashboards by having the CI pipeline automatically publish results after every run - build number, pass/fail, duration, environment and trend - into a tool such as Jenkins, GitLab, Allure, Grafana, ReportPortal or a TestOps platform. I treat them as living documents: each run updates the data automatically, and I verify the feed so the numbers stay trustworthy. I design them for the audience - a quick health summary for the team plus drill-down into failures with logs, screenshots and links to defects. I include trends over time so regressions, rising flakiness and slowing execution are obvious. I also configure alerts for critical failures so problems surface immediately rather than at the next stand-up.
questions.realTimeExample: Our nightly pipeline pushed results to a ReportPortal dashboard that showed pass rate, duration and new failures per suite. When execution time crept from 20 to 35 minutes over a week, the trend view flagged it and we optimised the slowest suite before it delayed releases.

questions.question: How do you process test-execution data?
questions.answer: I process execution data as a pipeline: the test runner emits machine-readable results (JUnit XML, JSON or HTML), the CI server collects and stores them, and a reporting layer parses and aggregates the data. I normalise results into a consistent schema so pass/fail, duration, environment, suite and test name can be compared across runs, then compute metrics such as pass rate, flakiness and trend deltas. I filter out known-broken tests and classify each failure as a genuine bug, an environment issue or a test defect, so the signal stays clean. This feed powers dashboards, alerts and automated release gates without manual effort. Finally I retain historical data for trend and audit purposes and regularly review failures to fix or quarantine flaky tests.
questions.realTimeExample: Our test framework exported JUnit XML after every run, which the CI job parsed into a database and displayed in a dashboard. Because each failure was tagged by category, we could instantly separate real regressions from environment flakes and focus triage on genuine bugs.

questions.question: We ship three times a day. Where does QA live in that cycle?
questions.answer: When a team ships three times a day, QA shifts left and becomes continuous rather than a pre-release phase. I work ahead of development by refining acceptance criteria and building automation that runs in the pipeline on every commit, so most verification happens automatically before merge. I rely on risk-based, targeted regression rather than a huge manual suite, and use feature flags, canary releases and automated smoke tests to validate each deployment quickly. Manual and exploratory testing is reserved for high-risk or complex areas and coordinated with short release windows. Quality becomes a shared, pipeline-embedded responsibility, and I own the test strategy, coverage and fast feedback loops that make frequent shipping safe. The goal is to make quality a continuous, automated signal rather than a late gate.
questions.realTimeExample: On a high-frequency SaaS release cycle, every merge triggered unit, API and smoke tests automatically, and deploys went out behind feature flags with canary monitoring. I focused my manual effort on new high-risk flows and edge cases, while automation caught most regressions within minutes of each commit.

questions.question: A flaky test let a bug reach production. Who owns that?
questions.answer: Everyone shares accountability for release quality, but as the quality owner I treat a flaky test as a serious defect in the test suite and drive its fix. An ignored flaky test erodes trust in the whole suite and can silently let real bugs through, so it must be triaged and stabilised, not simply muted or re-run until green. Typical root causes are timing and synchronisation issues, shared or order-dependent state, unmanaged test data, or environment instability. I own investigating and hardening the test - better waits, isolation, deterministic data - and I communicate the risk to the team. If the flake let a defect escape, we also review how the failure was triaged and add safeguards so a red result blocks the pipeline. Ownership is collective, but accountability for suite reliability sits with QA and automation.
questions.realTimeExample: A checkout test failed intermittently and was habitually re-run until it passed, masking a genuine race condition that later hit production. We quarantined it, fixed the synchronisation issue, and made unexplained re-runs a flagged anti-pattern so a real failure could no longer hide behind flakiness.

questions.question: Can you explain the services involved in the product you test?
questions.answer: I map the product's architecture so testing covers every layer and integration point, not just the UI. Typically that includes a front-end or client, a set of back-end microservices or APIs behind a gateway, databases and caches, message queues or event streams, and third-party or external dependencies. I also account for supporting services such as authentication and identity, payments, notifications, search and file storage, plus infrastructure like load balancers and CDNs. Knowing which service owns which behaviour lets me design meaningful integration, contract and failure-mode tests rather than only single-service checks. I often sketch a simple service and data-flow diagram to identify dependencies and pinpoint where integration risk is highest.
questions.realTimeExample: For an e-commerce app I mapped the storefront, product and order microservices, a cart cache, a payment gateway and a notification service. That map showed the order-to-payment handoff carried the most risk, so I prioritised integration and timeout tests exactly there.

questions.question: How do you handle compliance-bound test data management and data privacy?
questions.answer: For compliance-bound testing I never use real production personal data; instead I use synthetic data, anonymised or masked subsets, and format-preserving pseudonymisation so tests still behave realistically. I classify data by sensitivity - PII, PCI, PHI, GDPR - and apply the matching controls, keeping test data confined to approved environments with strict access restrictions. Where regulations apply, I ensure consent, retention limits, right-to-erasure and audit trails are respected in test environments too, not just production. I rely on data-generation and masking tooling so sensitive fields look realistic in shape but are fake in value. Any masked production copy is time-boxed, logged and approved, and I document the data-handling approach so it stands up to audit.
questions.realTimeExample: For a healthcare app covering HIPAA data, we generated synthetic patient records and masked any production extracts so names, IDs and diagnoses were fake but structurally valid. Access to the masked data was restricted and logged, and our approach passed the compliance team's audit without findings.

questions.question: An automation tester on your team refuses to do manual testing. How do you handle it?
questions.answer: I would treat this as a leadership and mindset issue rather than a purely technical one. First I would have a private conversation to understand the resistance, which is often about perceived status or workload rather than principle, and explain that manual, exploratory and usability testing remain essential for defects automation cannot reach. I would set clear expectations: a strong SDET does both, and refusing a needed activity affects the team's ability to ship quality software. If the gap is skill or confidence, I would coach and pair them on exploratory sessions to build capability. If, after documented expectations, it is a genuine attitude problem, I would escalate to their manager with evidence. The aim is to win the person over through purpose, growth and clear standards rather than to punish them.
questions.realTimeExample: An automation engineer on my team pushed back on exploratory testing, seeing it as beneath the role. After pairing him on a session where he found a high-impact usability bug automation had missed, his view shifted and he began volunteering for exploratory passes on risky features.

questions.question: Would you be comfortable doing manual testing, or writing unit-level tests in a programming language alongside developers, if the project needs it?
questions.answer: Yes - I am comfortable doing manual testing and writing unit-level tests whenever the project needs it. Good QA engineers stay versatile: exploratory and manual testing catch usability, edge-case and unknown-unknown issues that automation misses, while unit tests written alongside developers shift quality left and prevent bugs at the source. I can pair with developers, learn their language and frameworks such as JUnit, Jest or pytest, and contribute meaningful tests rather than throwaway ones. I coordinate with the team so we do not duplicate coverage, usually leaving unit tests to developers and focusing my automation on API, integration and UI layers. Ultimately I do whatever delivers the best quality outcome for the project.
questions.realTimeExample: On one project a new service had thin unit coverage, so I paired with the developer and added unit tests for boundary conditions in the same repository. In another, I spent a full day doing exploratory testing on a new UI and found accessibility issues automation would never have flagged.

questions.question: How do you collaborate with your team, and can you work as an individual contributor?
questions.answer: I collaborate continuously: I join refinement, planning and stand-ups, pair with developers on testability and automation, review requirements with the Product Owner, and share blameless quality feedback in reviews and retrospectives. I keep communication clear and use shared artefacts like tickets, dashboards and defect reports so everyone sees the same picture. At the same time I can work effectively as an individual contributor, owning test strategy, automation frameworks and end-to-end quality for a feature without constant supervision. I balance the two by defaulting to collaboration but taking full ownership of my deliverables and blockers. That mix keeps quality embedded in the team while ensuring clear accountability for outcomes.
questions.realTimeExample: While leading automation for a new module I designed and built the test framework independently, yet ran weekly syncs with developers and the Product Owner to align on acceptance criteria and catch integration risks early. The feature shipped with high confidence and no critical defects.

questions.question: What is the 'message house' technique?
questions.answer: The message house is a communication and alignment technique that structures key messages into a simple house shape: one overarching roof message (the core idea), supported by three or four pillars (the main supporting points), all resting on a foundation of facts, evidence or proof points. It forces you to lead with the headline, group supporting arguments logically, and back each with concrete data rather than rambling detail. In QA and Agile contexts it is useful for release notes, status reports, test-summary reports and stakeholder updates, so a reader grasps the message in seconds. It follows the pyramid-principle structure of conclusion first, then supporting detail. It pairs well with other structured techniques like STAR and the 30-second pitch for interviews and reporting.
questions.realTimeExample: When presenting a test-summary report I used a message house: the roof was 'the release is ready to ship', the pillars were test coverage, defect status and performance results, and the foundation was the underlying metrics and evidence. Stakeholders understood our readiness position in under a minute.

questions.question: Write a query for the Nth highest salary (2nd and 3rd, with employee name), with and without LIMIT/TOP.
questions.answer: Finding the Nth highest salary is a classic SQL problem that can be solved with several approaches. The simplest is ORDER BY salary DESC with LIMIT/OFFSET in MySQL/PostgreSQL (or TOP with an offset or subquery in SQL Server). The portable and safest approach that also works when you only need a specific rank is a correlated subquery using COUNT(DISTINCT salary) so ties do not break the result. Window functions such as DENSE_RANK() are the modern, cleanest way and handle duplicates in salary gracefully. For ranking rows (not distinct salaries) use ROW_NUMBER(), and use DENSE_RANK() when ties should share the same rank. Always add a deterministic tie-breaker such as ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id so results are reproducible. Below are both the LIMIT/TOP variants and the ranking variant.
questions.realTimeExample: In an HR analytics dashboard the test lead needs to verify the second and third highest-paid employees are shown correctly. Using LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 and DENSE_RANK() side by side lets QA cross-check that both the legacy and modern queries return the same employees.
questions.code:
-- MySQL / PostgreSQL: Nth highest salary with LIMIT/OFFSET
SELECT employee_name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;   -- 2nd highest, OFFSET 2 for 3rd

-- SQL Server: TOP with subquery
SELECT TOP 1 employee_name, salary
FROM (SELECT TOP 2 employee_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC) t
ORDER BY salary ASC;  -- 2nd highest

-- Portable: correlated subquery (handles ties via DISTINCT)
SELECT employee_name, salary
FROM employees e
WHERE 2 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM employees x WHERE x.salary > e.salary);

-- Modern: window function, works for any N
SELECT employee_name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT employee_name, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) ranked
WHERE rnk IN (2, 3);

questions.question: Write a query to find duplicate records, including duplicates across multiple columns.
questions.answer: Duplicate detection relies on GROUP BY combined with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, because HAVING filters aggregated groups after grouping. For single-column duplicates you group by that column; for duplicates across multiple columns you group by the whole combination (for example first_name plus email). If you also need to list the offending rows with their primary keys, wrap the grouped result in a subquery or use a self-join or ROW_NUMBER() partition. The self-join compares rows on the duplicate key and keeps pairs where the id differs, and ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY id) lets you flag every row after the first. This is essential in test data cleanup and data-quality checks.
questions.realTimeExample: Before a release, QA checks the customers table for duplicate emails created by a race condition in sign-up. The single-column query surfaces the duplicated email, and the multi-column query also catches users duplicated by name and phone.
questions.code:
-- Single-column duplicates
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS occurrences
FROM customers
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Duplicates across multiple columns
SELECT first_name, last_name, email, COUNT(*) AS occurrences
FROM customers
GROUP BY first_name, last_name, email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- List every duplicate row with its id using a self-join
SELECT c.*
FROM customers c
JOIN (
  SELECT email FROM customers GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
) d ON c.email = d.email
ORDER BY c.email;

-- Flag all duplicates with ROW_NUMBER
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT id, email,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn
  FROM customers
) t
WHERE rn > 1;

questions.question: Write a query to find employees who have never placed an order.
questions.answer: Employees with no orders are found by comparing the two tables and keeping rows that have no matching order. The clearest approaches are NOT EXISTS (usually the most efficient and NULL-safe), LEFT JOIN with IS NULL, or NOT IN (which must be used carefully because a NULL in the subquery returns no rows). NOT EXISTS is preferred because it short-circuits and ignores NULLs correctly. These anti-join patterns apply to any parent/child relationship such as customers without invoices or products never sold. Always confirm the join key is indexed for performance on large tables.
questions.realTimeExample: An e-commerce team wants to nudge salespeople who have never closed an order. QA validates the 'no orders yet' report by running NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN versions and confirming both return the same employee list.
questions.code:
-- Preferred: NOT EXISTS
SELECT e.employee_id, e.employee_name
FROM employees e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.employee_id = e.employee_id
);

-- LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
SELECT e.employee_id, e.employee_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.employee_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

-- NOT IN (be careful with NULLs in the subquery)
SELECT employee_id, employee_name
FROM employees
WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM orders);

questions.question: Explain SQL joins and their types, inner vs outer join, and a real project use case; write a JOIN across two given tables.
questions.answer: A join combines rows from two or more tables using a related column, usually a primary-key to foreign-key relation. INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matches from the right (unmatched right columns become NULL), RIGHT JOIN does the mirror image, and FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both. CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product, and SELF JOIN joins a table to itself. The key difference is that inner join discards non-matching rows while outer joins preserve them. In testing, joins are essential to verify that data written in one table is correctly reflected in a related table.
questions.realTimeExample: In an order management system, QA joins the orders table to the customers table to confirm every order shows the correct customer name, and uses a LEFT JOIN to find orders whose customer record is missing.
questions.code:
-- Tables: customers(customer_id, customer_name), orders(order_id, customer_id, amount)

-- INNER JOIN: only customers who have orders
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

-- LEFT JOIN: all customers, even those without orders
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

-- RIGHT JOIN: all orders, even orphaned ones without a customer
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

-- FULL OUTER JOIN (PostgreSQL/SQL Server)
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

questions.question: What is the use of GROUP BY? Write a query to count employees per department.
questions.answer: GROUP BY collapses rows that share the same values in the grouped columns into a single row, letting aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX operate per group. Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT must appear in the GROUP BY clause. It is typically paired with HAVING to filter groups after aggregation, whereas WHERE filters rows before aggregation. GROUP BY is the backbone of summary and reporting queries and is frequently used by testers to validate counts against expected business rules. The query below counts how many employees belong to each department.
questions.realTimeExample: An HR test validates a headcount report by counting employees per department in the database and comparing the numbers to the figures shown on the dashboard.
questions.code:
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
ORDER BY employee_count DESC;

-- With department name via join and filtering groups
SELECT d.department_name, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS employee_count
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_name
HAVING COUNT(e.employee_id) > 5
ORDER BY employee_count DESC;

questions.question: Write a query for the maximum salary in each department.
questions.answer: To get the maximum salary per department you group rows by department and apply MAX(salary) to each group. This returns one row per department with its highest salary. If you also need the employee who earns that maximum, you either join the grouped result back to the employees table on both department and salary, or use a window function such as RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) and keep rank = 1. The grouped approach is the simplest for a pure per-group maximum, while the window approach is cleaner when you need the full row. Testers use this to verify compensation reports match the source data.
questions.realTimeExample: A payroll audit requires the top salary in each department. QA runs the grouped query and the RANK() version and confirms both return identical department-and-salary pairs before signing off the report.
questions.code:
-- Simplest: MAX per department
SELECT department_id, MAX(salary) AS max_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id;

-- Max salary plus the employee who earns it
SELECT e.department_id, e.employee_name, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN (
  SELECT department_id, MAX(salary) AS max_salary
  FROM employees
  GROUP BY department_id
) m ON e.department_id = m.department_id AND e.salary = m.max_salary;

-- Window function alternative
SELECT department_id, employee_name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT department_id, employee_name, salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) t
WHERE rnk = 1;

questions.question: Write a query to retrieve the details of the employee with the highest salary.
questions.answer: To return the full row of the highest-paid employee, the simplest approach is ORDER BY salary DESC with LIMIT 1 (or TOP 1 in SQL Server). Because ties are possible, a more robust option is to filter with salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees), which returns every employee tied for the maximum. If you only ever want a single deterministic row, add a tie-breaker column to the ORDER BY. Avoid relying on MAX alone in a non-grouped SELECT because it would mix an aggregate with ungrouped columns. The subquery form is the safest when confirming the top earner in a data-accuracy check.
questions.realTimeExample: An HR dashboard shows the top earner. QA confirms the displayed employee matches the database by running the ORDER BY and MAX subquery versions and checking they agree.
questions.code:
-- MySQL / PostgreSQL
SELECT *
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1;

-- SQL Server
SELECT TOP 1 *
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;

-- Handles ties: returns all employees at the max salary
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

questions.question: Write a query for employees who joined in the last 30 days.
questions.answer: To find recent joiners you filter the joining date column against a rolling window of the last 30 days. The portable way is joining_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30' DAY (PostgreSQL) or >= DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) in MySQL, or >= DATEADD(DAY, -30, GETDATE()) in SQL Server. Using fixed dates in tests is fragile, so parameterizing or computing from the current date keeps the query stable. This pattern is used for onboarding dashboards and probation reminders. Always confirm the column is a date/datetime type so the comparison is not affected by time-of-day.
questions.realTimeExample: An HR onboarding report lists employees who started in the last 30 days so IT can provision accounts. QA runs the query and cross-checks the count against the report's figure for today's date.
questions.code:
-- MySQL
SELECT employee_id, employee_name, joining_date
FROM employees
WHERE joining_date >= DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY);

-- PostgreSQL
SELECT employee_id, employee_name, joining_date
FROM employees
WHERE joining_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30' DAY;

-- SQL Server
SELECT employee_id, employee_name, joining_date
FROM employees
WHERE joining_date >= DATEADD(DAY, -30, GETDATE());

questions.question: Write a query to select even roll numbers from a student table.
questions.answer: Even roll numbers are selected using the modulo operator, checking the remainder of the roll number divided by 2 equals 0. In standard SQL the modulo is the MOD() function, and most databases also support the % operator. The same technique works for odd numbers by testing remainder = 1, and for multiples of any number by adjusting the divisor. This is a common screening/interview query that demonstrates arithmetic operators and filtering. If roll_number is stored as text, cast it to an integer first so the arithmetic comparison works correctly.
questions.realTimeExample: In a small demo database of students, QA verifies a report that lists students assigned to alternating lab batches by filtering on even roll numbers.
questions.code:
-- Standard SQL using MOD()
SELECT roll_number, student_name
FROM students
WHERE MOD(roll_number, 2) = 0;

-- Using the % operator (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server)
SELECT roll_number, student_name
FROM students
WHERE roll_number % 2 = 0;

-- Odd roll numbers
SELECT roll_number, student_name
FROM students
WHERE MOD(roll_number, 2) = 1;

questions.question: Write a query to select all unique names from a student table.
questions.answer: SELECT DISTINCT returns only unique values for the selected columns, removing duplicate rows from the result set. DISTINCT applies to the whole selected column list, so selecting two columns returns unique combinations, not unique values per column. An alternative for a single column is GROUP BY, which groups identical values and is often used when you also want a count. DISTINCT is a row-level filter and does not affect the underlying table. Use it carefully on large tables because it can be expensive without proper indexing.
questions.realTimeExample: A university report needs a deduplicated list of enrolled student names for a circular. QA runs SELECT DISTINCT student_name and compares the count to the list to confirm no names are repeated.

questions.question: What is the difference between DDL and DML?
questions.answer: DDL (Data Definition Language) defines and modifies the structure of database objects, including CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE and RENAME statements. DML (Data Manipulation Language) works with the data inside those objects, including INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT. DDL changes are typically auto-committed and cannot be rolled back in many databases, whereas DML changes can be committed or rolled back within a transaction. DDL affects the schema (tables, columns, indexes), while DML affects the rows. Testers care about this distinction because accidental DDL can permanently alter a test environment, while DML mistakes can be safely reverted. Both are essential for setting up and validating test data.
questions.realTimeExample: During test setup QA runs DML INSERTs to create users and can roll them back if something fails, but a DDL ALTER that adds a column is permanent and is coordinated with the DBA to avoid breaking other tests.

questions.question: What are subqueries used for?
questions.answer: A subquery is a query nested inside another statement, used to return a value, a list of values, or a derived table that the outer query consumes. Scalar subqueries return a single value (useful in WHERE or SELECT), while row and table subqueries are compared with IN, EXISTS, ANY or ALL. Correlated subqueries reference columns from the outer query and run once per outer row, which is powerful but can be slow on large data. Subqueries are commonly used for finding maxima/minima, checking existence, and feeding computed filters. They can often be rewritten as joins for better performance, so a good answer mentions both forms.
questions.realTimeExample: A tester writes a scalar subquery to fetch employees earning above the company average salary and validates the result against an independently computed list of names.

questions.question: How many unique/primary keys can a table have, and how do primary and foreign keys relate?
questions.answer: A table can have only one primary key, but that key may span multiple columns (a composite primary key). Unique keys, by contrast, can be multiple per table; a unique constraint also enforces uniqueness but allows a single NULL (depending on the database) and does not necessarily make the column the table's identifier. A primary key is not nullable and creates a clustered index by default in many databases, while a unique key is nullable and non-clustered by default. A foreign key is a column (or set of columns) in one table that references the primary key (or a unique key) of another, enforcing referential integrity. This relationship lets child rows point to a valid parent row and prevents orphaned records. Testers verify these constraints by attempting to insert duplicates or invalid foreign keys and confirming the database rejects them.
questions.realTimeExample: In an e-commerce schema, orders.order_id is the primary key of orders, customers.customer_id is the primary key of customers, and orders.customer_id is a foreign key referencing customers; QA confirms an order cannot be inserted with a non-existent customer_id.

questions.question: Explain a complex SQL query you wrote in your project, and other queries you run day to day.
questions.answer: For a complex query, describe the business goal first, then the tables and joins, the filters, the aggregation or window functions, and what you validated. A common example is a reconciliation query that joins orders, payments and refunds with LEFT JOINs, groups by customer, and uses CASE plus SUM to compute net revenue while highlighting mismatches. Day-to-day tester queries are usually simpler: validating a record exists, counting rows to match an expected total, checking status transitions, and confirming foreign keys. The key is showing you can explain the logic clearly and tie every query to a testable assertion. Emphasize CTEs for readability and that you avoid SELECT * in production checks.
questions.realTimeExample: In a payments project QA wrote a CTE-based reconciliation query that compares captured payments against order totals per day; it flagged three orders where the captured amount did not match, which became a high-priority bug. Day to day QA also runs count and existence checks after each API regression run.
questions.code:
WITH captured AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS captured_amt
  FROM payments
  WHERE status = 'CAPTURED'
  GROUP BY order_id
),
refunded AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS refunded_amt
  FROM refunds
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.total_amount,
       COALESCE(c.captured_amt, 0) AS captured,
       COALESCE(r.refunded_amt, 0) AS refunded,
       o.total_amount - COALESCE(c.captured_amt, 0) AS mismatch
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN captured c ON c.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN refunded r ON r.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.total_amount <> COALESCE(c.captured_amt, 0)
ORDER BY mismatch DESC;

-- Day-to-day: count check and existence check
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING';
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE order_id = 1001;

questions.question: What are database validation concepts?
questions.answer: Database validation is the practice of confirming that data stored in the database is accurate, complete, consistent and conforms to the application's business rules. It covers constraint checks (primary, unique, foreign, not-null, check constraints), data-type and length validation, referential integrity, and business-rule validation such as status values or numeric ranges. Testers verify these by writing queries that compare expected versus actual rows, counts, and values, and by attempting invalid inserts to confirm the database rejects them. It also includes cross-table reconciliation, ensuring derived values match source data. Good validation combines positive tests (valid data is accepted) with negative tests (invalid data is rejected).
questions.realTimeExample: For a banking app, QA validates that a transfer updates both the sender and receiver balances, that no negative balances exist, and that a duplicate transaction reference is rejected by a unique constraint.

questions.question: How do you validate UI data against database values, e.g. records after a UI checkout?
questions.answer: UI-to-database validation means capturing the exact values shown on the screen and independently querying the database for the same logical record, then comparing every field. For a checkout you would note the order id, item, quantity, unit price, tax, discount and grand total in the UI, then query the orders and order_items tables and assert each field matches, including computed totals. Always isolate the correct record using a unique key such as the order id or the most recent timestamp for that user, and mind rounding rules for currency. Validation should also cover dependent records, for example inventory decrement and payment rows created alongside the order. Automate the comparison using a framework like Selenium or Playwright plus a JDBC/database library so the check is repeatable.
questions.realTimeExample: After a test checkout, QA reads the confirmation page total of 118.00, then runs a query joining orders and order_items and asserts subtotal + tax equals the displayed total and that exactly one payment row was created.
questions.code:
-- Verify the order header and items created by a UI checkout
SELECT o.order_id, o.status, o.subtotal, o.tax, o.discount, o.grand_total,
       i.item_name, i.quantity, i.unit_price, (i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS line_total
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_id = 1001;

-- Assert that stored grand_total equals computed subtotal + tax - discount
SELECT order_id, grand_total, (subtotal + tax - discount) AS computed
FROM orders
WHERE order_id = 1001
  AND grand_total <> (subtotal + tax - discount);  -- expect zero rows

-- Confirm exactly one payment row exists for the checkout
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE order_id = 1001;

questions.question: How do you validate data consistently across API, application and database?
questions.answer: Consistent cross-layer validation starts by identifying the same logical entity at each layer: the API response payload, the application/service state, and the rows in the database. You then compare equivalent fields using unique identifiers so you match the same record everywhere, checking values, types, formats (dates, currency) and counts. A typical flow is to trigger an action through the API, capture the JSON response, query the database for the affected rows, and assert the response fields equal the stored values. Differences often come from caching, async processing, or transformation layers, so you must allow for eventual consistency where the system is asynchronous. Automating this in the API test suite by asserting response versus a JDBC query gives continuous, reliable coverage.
questions.realTimeExample: In a microservices project QA creates a user via POST /users, gets the JSON with the generated id, then queries the users table to confirm name, email and status match, and re-fetches via GET /users/{id} to confirm the API and database agree.

questions.question: The database shows one value, the API returns another and the UI displays a third. How do you find the source of the issue?
questions.answer: When three layers disagree, you work bottom-up to isolate where the value changes. First capture ground truth from the database with a query filtered by the record's unique id. Next call the API directly (for example with Postman or curl) and inspect the raw JSON. Finally inspect the UI's network tab to see what the browser actually received versus what it rendered. If the API already differs from the database, the bug is in the API/service or the query it uses; if the API matches the database but the UI differs, the bug is in the frontend or a caching/transformation layer. Comparing each pair (DB vs API, API vs UI) localises the layer. Also rule out stale caches, joins, or multiple data sources feeding different layers.
questions.realTimeExample: An order total showed 100.00 in the DB, 120.00 from the API and 110.00 in the UI. QA found the API applied a stale tax rate from a cache-less legacy service, and the UI applied an outdated client-side rounding rule, so two separate defects were logged.
questions.code:
-- Step 1: database ground truth
SELECT order_id, subtotal, tax, grand_total, updated_at
FROM orders WHERE order_id = 1001;

-- Step 2: call the API directly
-- curl -s https://api.example.com/orders/1001

-- Step 3: inspect the UI network tab (DevTools) for the same request/response

-- Step 4: check for alternate data sources that might feed a layer
SELECT * FROM order_totals_cache WHERE order_id = 1001;   -- suspicious cache table?

questions.question: After clicking Submit, the data is not updated in the database. How do you troubleshoot the root cause?
questions.answer: First confirm whether the request even reached the backend by checking the browser Network tab for the Submit call, its status code and payload. If the request failed (4xx/5xx) or was never sent, the problem is client-side or a validation block; if it succeeded (200/201), the problem is server-side persistence. Then inspect the application and API logs for exceptions, transaction rollbacks or validation errors, and confirm you are querying the correct database, schema and environment. Check whether the write targets a different table, is committed in a transaction that later rolls back, or is blocked by a constraint. Also verify you are not looking at a read replica, a cached view, or the wrong record id. Reproduce with the same user and data to isolate whether it is data-specific.
questions.realTimeExample: A tester clicks Submit on a profile update and sees no change in the database. The Network tab shows a 200 response, but the API logs reveal a silent catch that discarded the update; the fix was in the service layer, not the database.

questions.question: A critical API returns a valid response but the UI shows blank screens for some users. How do you trace it across API, data and UI layers?
questions.answer: Start by characterising 'some users' - identify what is common to the affected accounts (role, region, tenant, feature flag, or a specific data shape) because that points to a filtering or permission rule. Compare the API response for an affected user versus a working user and look for subtle differences such as an empty array, a missing field, or a different data type that the UI fails to handle. Check the browser console for JavaScript errors and inspect the network tab to confirm the UI received data it could not render. Then go to the database to see whether the affected users actually have the expected rows, or whether a query/permission filter is returning nothing. The likely culprit is either a data gap for those users or a frontend null/empty-handling bug triggered by valid-but-unexpected data.
questions.realTimeExample: Blank dashboards affected only users in one region. The API returned an empty transactions array for them because a timezone filter in the query excluded their records; the UI rendered blank instead of an empty state, exposing a second defect.
questions.code:
-- 1. Identify the affected-user cohort (what differs)
SELECT region, role, feature_flag, COUNT(*) AS users
FROM users
GROUP BY region, role, feature_flag
ORDER BY users DESC;

-- 2. Check whether affected users even have the expected data
SELECT u.user_id, COUNT(t.transaction_id) AS txn_count
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN transactions t ON t.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE u.region = 'APAC'
GROUP BY u.user_id
ORDER BY txn_count ASC;

-- 3. Confirm a filter/timezone rule is not excluding their rows
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM transactions
WHERE user_id = 901 AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90' DAY;

-- 4. Compare raw API output for one broken vs one working user (Postman/DevTools)

questions.question: How do you connect to a database with JDBC, run queries and assert row counts? Write the connection code.
questions.answer: JDBC connects Java code to any relational database through a URL, driver and credentials. You load the driver, obtain a Connection, create a PreparedStatement to avoid SQL injection, execute a query returning a ResultSet, and iterate to count or read rows. Always close resources, preferably with try-with-resources, and externalize credentials rather than hardcoding them. In tests you then assert the row count or field values against expected values using an assertion library. PreparedStatement with bound parameters is the correct, secure pattern for parameterised test data.
questions.realTimeExample: In an API test suite QA verifies that creating an order through the API inserts exactly one row in the orders table; a JDBC helper runs SELECT COUNT(*) with the generated order id and asserts it equals 1.

questions.question: Write code to connect to MongoDB and extract an object.
questions.answer: MongoDB is accessed in Java through the MongoDB driver, which uses a connection string (mongodb://host:port) and a MongoClient. You get a database, then a collection, then build a Document filter to find the object you want; find() returns an iterable cursor while findOne() returns a single Document. You extract fields with getString, getInteger, getObjectId and similar accessors. Always close the client when done, preferably with try-with-resources, and store the connection string in configuration rather than code. In Python the equivalent uses pymongo with MongoClient and find_one. This is common for testing NoSQL-backed services where documents are not relational.
questions.realTimeExample: For a service that stores user profiles in MongoDB, QA connects with the driver, fetches the document for a specific user id after an API update, and asserts the stored email and status fields match the API response.

questions.question: How do you seed database preconditions before API suites and clean up test records afterwards?
questions.answer: Seeding means inserting the exact data an API test needs, such as a user, a product or an order, before the test runs, and cleanup means removing it afterwards so the suite is repeatable and isolated. The standard approach uses setup/teardown hooks (JUnit @BeforeAll/@AfterAll, TestNG @BeforeSuite, or pytest fixtures) that insert via SQL or the API itself, capture the generated unique ids, and delete those ids in teardown. Prefer creating data through APIs where possible so business rules and constraints are respected, falling back to direct SQL inserts for speed when needed. Use unique, prefixed identifiers or transactions you can roll back to avoid collisions between parallel tests. Never rely on a shared fixed record that other tests might mutate, and always clean up in the correct order to respect foreign-key constraints.
questions.realTimeExample: Before an API regression suite, QA seeds a test customer and a product with a timestamped email, runs the tests against those ids, then deletes the orders, then the product, then the customer in teardown so the order of foreign keys is respected.

questions.question: How would you perform backend testing without running queries?
questions.answer: Backend testing without direct SQL is possible by validating through the layers that expose data and behaviour. You test the API endpoints, inspect their JSON responses, status codes and error messages for correctness, and rely on the application's own validation, constraints and error handling as observable behaviour. You can also use logs, audit trails, application-level reports and the UI as indirect evidence of what was persisted. SoapUI/Postman collections, contract tests, and integration tests that call service methods directly all exercise backend logic without writing queries. The database can still be inspected indirectly through APIs that expose resources, or through health and admin endpoints. The trade-off is you lose direct ground-truth verification, so this approach complements rather than fully replaces SQL checking.
questions.realTimeExample: When a team's DB access was restricted to DBAs, QA validated a new order flow purely through the REST API: create order, re-fetch it, list orders, and confirm audit logs and error codes, all without SQL access.
questions.code:
-- No SQL used. Internet validation is done via API calls and assertions:

# 1. Create
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/orders \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"customerId": 42, "amount": 118.00}'

# 2. Read back and assert the persisted state via the API
curl https://api.example.com/orders/1001

# 3. List and assert the record appears
curl https://api.example.com/customers/42/orders

# 4. Negative / error handling checks
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/orders \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"customerId": 999999, "amount": 10}'   # expect 400/404 with clear error

# 5. Indirect evidence: audit-log endpoint
curl https://api.example.com/audit?entity=order&id=1001

questions.question: What are the stages of committing code, and the steps/commands to commit and push (git add, git commit, git diff, git push, git pull)?
questions.answer: Git moves changes through three main areas: the working directory, the staging area (index), and the local repository. You edit files in the working directory, then use `git add` to stage the specific changes you want in your next commit. `git commit` then records everything staged into the local repository as a new snapshot with a message. `git push` uploads your local commits to the remote branch, and `git pull` fetches remote changes and merges them into your current branch to keep you up to date. It is good practice to run `git status` and `git diff` before staging to review what changed, and `git diff --staged` after adding to confirm exactly what will be committed.
questions.realTimeExample: When I finished fixing a login validation bug, I ran `git status` to see the modified files, `git diff` to review the change, then `git add LoginPage.js`, committed with a clear message, pulled the latest main branch, and pushed to my feature branch for review.
questions.code:
git status
git diff
git add file1.js file2.js
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Fix login validation bug"
git pull origin main
git push origin feature/login-fix

questions.question: Is git push origin feature-branch correct? Why?
questions.answer: Yes, `git push origin feature-branch` is correct when origin is the name of your remote and feature-branch is the branch you want to publish. `origin` is simply the default alias for the remote repository URL that Git created during clone, and the second argument is the local branch name to push to the matching remote branch. If the branch does not yet exist on the remote, this command creates it there; adding `-u` (as in `git push -u origin feature-branch`) also sets the upstream so future `git push` and `git pull` work without repeating the arguments. If the remote is named differently, such as `upstream` in a fork workflow, you would substitute that name instead.
questions.realTimeExample: On a fork-based project, I created a branch, committed my fix, and ran `git push -u origin fix/header-nav` so that the branch appeared on my fork and later a pull request could be opened against the main repository.
questions.code:
git checkout -b feature-branch
git push -u origin feature-branch

questions.question: What is the difference between git fetch, git pull and git clone?
questions.answer: `git clone` is used once to create a full copy of an existing remote repository locally, including its history and remote configuration. `git fetch` downloads new commits, branches, and tags from the remote into your local remote-tracking branches but does not touch your working directory, so your files stay exactly as they are. `git pull` is essentially `git fetch` followed by a `git merge` (or rebase, if configured), so it both downloads and immediately integrates the remote changes into your current branch. In short, clone creates a repository, fetch updates your view of the remote safely, and pull updates and merges in one step.
questions.realTimeExample: Before starting work each morning I run `git fetch` to see if teammates pushed anything, review the incoming commits with `git log origin/main`, and only then run `git pull` to actually merge those changes into my branch.
questions.code:
git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git
git fetch origin
git log origin/main --oneline
git pull origin main

questions.question: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase, and when do you use rebase?
questions.answer: `git merge` combines two branches by creating a new merge commit that joins their histories, preserving the exact branch topology. `git rebase` instead replays your commits on top of another branch, producing a linear history without an extra merge commit. Rebase gives a cleaner, easier-to-read log but rewrites commit hashes, so it must never be used on branches that others have already pulled. You typically use rebase to keep a short-lived feature branch current with main before opening a pull request, or to squash and tidy local commits, while merge is preferred for integrating finished features into shared long-lived branches.
questions.realTimeExample: While working on a feature over several days, I ran `git rebase main` regularly so my branch stayed on top of the latest main changes and my pull request history remained linear and conflict-free.
questions.code:
git checkout feature
git rebase main
# resolve conflicts, then:
git add <file>
git rebase --continue

questions.question: How do you resolve merge/rebase conflicts during an active sprint?
questions.answer: When Git reports a conflict, I first run `git status` to list the affected files and open each one to locate the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers. I carefully decide which changes to keep, often combining both sides, then remove the markers and save the file. After editing I run `git add` on the resolved files and continue with `git commit` for a merge or `git rebase --continue` for a rebase; if things go wrong I can abort with `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` to return to the previous state. To reduce future conflicts I pull or rebase frequently and keep branches small and short-lived.
questions.realTimeExample: Mid-sprint two developers edited the same config file, so when I rebased I opened it, merged both configuration blocks, removed the conflict markers, staged the file, and continued the rebase, then verified the feature still built before pushing.
questions.code:
git status
git merge --abort
git rebase --abort
git add <file>
git rebase --continue

questions.question: What does git stash do, and how do you apply stashed changes back?
questions.answer: `git stash` temporarily shelves your uncommitted changes (both staged and unstaged) so your working directory returns to a clean state without committing anything. This is handy when you need to switch branches, pull urgent fixes, or test something else without losing work in progress. You bring the changes back with `git stash apply`, which restores them but keeps the stash entry, or `git stash pop`, which restores and removes the entry in one step. `git stash list` shows all saved stashes, and you can target a specific one with `git stash apply stash@{n}` when you have more than one.
questions.realTimeExample: I was halfway through a refactor when a critical production bug needed an immediate fix, so I stashed my work, switched to the hotfix branch, fixed and pushed the bug, then returned and popped the stash to continue where I left off.
questions.code:
git stash
git stash list
git stash apply
git stash pop
git stash apply stash@{1}

questions.question: What is the use case of git cherry-pick?
questions.answer: `git cherry-pick` applies a specific commit from one branch onto your current branch by its commit hash, without merging the whole branch. It is useful when you need a single bug fix or feature from a branch that is not ready to be merged, such as copying a hotfix from a release branch into main. It also helps when a commit landed on the wrong branch and you want to move it elsewhere. The main caution is that cherry-picking creates a duplicate commit with a new hash, which can cause confusion or conflicts if the same change is later merged, so it should be used for targeted cases rather than routine integration.
questions.realTimeExample: A critical fix was committed to the develop branch, and I needed it in the production release branch that could not take the full branch, so I cherry-picked just that commit hash into the release branch and deployed the fix.
questions.code:
git checkout release
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d
# for a range:
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d^..f4e5d6c

questions.question: What Git branching strategies do you know, and which workflow do you follow?
questions.answer: Common strategies include Git Flow (long-lived develop and main branches with feature, release, and hotfix branches), GitHub Flow (a single main branch plus short-lived feature branches merged via pull requests), and trunk-based development (developers commit to main frequently with feature flags and short-lived branches). GitLab Flow and release-branch workflows are also popular for teams that need staged environments. In most of my agile projects I follow a GitHub Flow or trunk-based approach: create a feature branch off main, commit and push regularly, open a pull request, get a review with passing CI checks, and merge after approval. This keeps integration frequent, reduces merge pain, and aligns well with continuous delivery.
questions.realTimeExample: On my last team we used GitHub Flow: each ticket got a short-lived branch named after it, we opened a pull request early, CI ran the test suite automatically, and after one approval the branch was merged and deleted.
questions.code:
git checkout -b feature/JIRA-123
git push -u origin feature/JIRA-123
# after PR approval:
git checkout main
git pull
git branch -d feature/JIRA-123

questions.question: Is it possible to revert changes in a remote repository? How?
questions.answer: Yes, you can revert changes in a remote repository, but the safe and recommended way is to create a new commit that undoes the bad change rather than rewriting history. `git revert <commit>` generates an inverse commit that cancels the effect of a specific commit, and you then push it, which keeps the shared history intact and is safe for everyone. If you must remove the most recent commit entirely, you can use `git reset --hard HEAD~1` locally followed by a forced push (`git push --force-with-lease`), but this rewrites history and can break teammates who already pulled, so it should be avoided on shared branches. Choosing revert over force-push is the professional default on protected branches.
questions.realTimeExample: A faulty commit was pushed straight to main and broke the build, so instead of force-pushing I ran `git revert` on that commit, pushed the reverting commit through a quick PR, and the branch was healthy again without disrupting anyone's history.
questions.code:
git log --oneline
git revert <commit-hash>
git push origin main
# only if necessary on a private branch:
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git push --force-with-lease origin main

questions.question: Why do we need a .gitignore file, and how do you add files to it?
questions.answer: A `.gitignore` file tells Git which files and folders to exclude from version control, such as build artifacts, dependency folders like node_modules or target, IDE settings, and secrets like .env files. This keeps the repository clean, avoids committing generated or sensitive files, and prevents noisy diffs and accidental credential leaks. You add entries by creating or editing the `.gitignore` file at the repository root and listing file names, folder names, or glob patterns, one per line. If a file was already tracked before being ignored, you must untrack it with `git rm --cached` before the ignore rule takes effect.
questions.realTimeExample: Our repo had node_modules and log files being committed accidentally, so I added them to .gitignore, untracked the already-committed folder with `git rm -r --cached node_modules`, and committed the cleanup so future commits stayed clean.
questions.code:
echo "node_modules/" >> .gitignore
echo "target/" >> .gitignore
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git rm -r --cached node_modules
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Update gitignore"

questions.question: When do you commit your code, and how do you confirm everyone has the updated code?
questions.answer: I commit frequently with small, logically complete changes tied to a specific task, and I follow the team's message convention (often referencing the ticket ID) so history stays meaningful and reviewable. I commit once a unit of work compiles and passes locally, rather than bundling unrelated edits, which makes debugging and reverting much easier. To confirm everyone has the latest code, the team relies on the shared remote branch as the single source of truth: teammates pull regularly, and CI runs on every push so the whole team sees the build status. Merge or pull requests with automated checks and notifications ensure no one is left behind, and daily stand-ups surface any pending updates.
questions.realTimeExample: Our rule was to commit at least daily with a ticket reference like 'PROJ-451 Add retry logic', and since the pipeline ran on every push and notified the team channel, everyone knew the shared branch was current and green.
questions.code:
git add .
git commit -m "PROJ-451 Add retry logic to API client"
git pull --rebase origin main
git push origin feature/PROJ-451

questions.question: When you join a new project, which Git commands do you use from start to finish?
questions.answer: On joining a new project I first clone the repository with `git clone <url>`, then run `git status` and `git branch -a` to see the current state and available branches. I check out the working branch (usually main or develop) with `git checkout`, pull the latest changes, and create my own feature branch with `git checkout -b`. I then configure my identity if needed (`git config`), make changes, stage and commit them, and push the branch with `git push -u origin <branch>` to open a pull request. This start-to-finish flow gets me from cloning to contributing in a clean, standard way.
questions.realTimeExample: Onboarding onto a new repo, I cloned it, ran git status and git branch -a to orient myself, checked out develop, pulled the latest, created a branch for my first ticket, and pushed it as my first pull request.
questions.code:
git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git
git status
git branch -a
git checkout develop
git pull
git checkout -b feature/onboarding-task
git push -u origin feature/onboarding-task

questions.question: Explain your CI/CD execution flow - what happens end to end when a Jenkins build is triggered and runs your automated tests?
questions.answer: When a developer pushes code, Jenkins is triggered via a webhook or a polled SCM change and starts a job that checks out the latest source into a clean workspace. The pipeline then builds the project (for example `mvn clean install`), which compiles code and resolves dependencies, and may build a Docker image or deploy to a test environment. Next it runs the automated test suite - unit, integration, and UI tests - and captures reports like JUnit XML and screenshots on failure. Based on the outcome, Jenkins marks the build as success, unstable, or failed, publishes the results back to the pull request, and notifies the team via email or chat. If tests pass, later stages deploy to staging or production, completing the CI/CD flow.
questions.realTimeExample: In our project, a push to a feature branch triggered Jenkins automatically, which built the Maven project, ran Selenium regression on a Selenium grid, published the JUnit report, and posted pass or fail status straight back to the GitHub pull request.

questions.question: How do you integrate and run your test suite in Jenkins or GitHub Actions?
questions.answer: In Jenkins I integrate tests by making the automation project part of the Maven or Gradle build (or by invoking the test runner directly) and calling it from a pipeline stage, then archiving the reports with the `junit` step or publishing HTML reports. Credentials, browser versions, and environment URLs are passed as parameters or Jenkins credentials rather than hard-coded. In GitHub Actions I add a workflow YAML under `.github/workflows` that checks out the code, sets up the required language or browser, installs dependencies, and runs the test command, uploading reports and artifacts. Both approaches run the suite automatically on push and pull requests and surface results in the UI, and I typically parallelize or split suites to keep feedback fast.
questions.realTimeExample: We ran our Selenium suite through a Maven `test` command in a Jenkins pipeline and, after migrating, an equivalent GitHub Actions workflow that installed Chrome, ran the tests, and uploaded the Allure report as a build artifact.
questions.code:
name: test
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: '17' }
      - run: mvn -B test
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with: { name: test-reports, path: target/surefire-reports }

questions.question: What is the difference between Jenkins freestyle jobs and pipeline scripts? Can you create a pipeline from a script?
questions.answer: A freestyle job is configured entirely through the Jenkins UI with form fields and checkboxes, which is quick for simple tasks but hard to version, review, or reuse. A pipeline job defines the build as code in a Jenkinsfile using either declarative or scripted Groovy syntax, so the whole flow is stored in the repository, versioned, reviewed, and portable. Pipelines support complex logic, stages, parallelism, and shared libraries, making them far better suited to real CI/CD needs than freestyle jobs. Yes, you can absolutely create a pipeline from a script: you check in a Jenkinsfile and configure either a Pipeline job pointing to it (SCM) or a Multibranch Pipeline that auto-discovers Jenkinsfiles per branch.
questions.realTimeExample: Our team replaced several fragile freestyle jobs with a single Jenkinsfile in the repo, so any change to the build process went through a pull request and review instead of someone clicking around the Jenkins UI.

questions.question: How do you create a parameterized pipeline job and pass environment parameters into a build?
questions.answer: To create a parameterized pipeline job, you define a `parameters` block in the Jenkinsfile (or add parameters in the job configuration) with types such as string, choice, boolean, or credentials. The user supplies values when triggering the build, and Jenkins exposes them as environment variables accessible via `params.NAME` or `${env.NAME}` inside stages. You pass them down to scripts or tools by exporting them in a shell step, using `withEnv`, or referencing them in the command, and secrets should use the credentials or `withCredentials` binding rather than plain text. This makes a single job reusable across environments like dev, staging, and prod without duplicating configuration.
questions.realTimeExample: We ran one smoke-test job that took an environment choice parameter (qa, staging, prod) and a browser choice, so the same pipeline could target any environment without creating separate jobs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a CRON expression in Jenkins?
questions.answer: A CRON expression in Jenkins defines a schedule that tells the job when to run automatically, without waiting for a code push. It uses five space-separated fields (or an alias like `@daily`): minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. For example, `H 2 * * *` runs once daily around 2 AM, and the special `H` symbol tells Jenkins to spread the load by picking a consistent hashed minute rather than all jobs firing at once. This is useful for nightly regression runs, periodic health checks, or cleanup jobs, though it is important to note Jenkins uses the server's timezone by default.
questions.realTimeExample: We scheduled a nightly cron at `H 1 * * *` so our full regression suite ran every night, and developers saw fresh results each morning without anyone manually starting the job.
questions.code:
H 1 * * *        // once daily, hashed minute, at ~1 AM
H/15 * * * *     // every 15 minutes
0 8 * * MON-FRI  // 8:00 AM on weekdays

questions.question: What is the difference between Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
questions.answer: Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of merging code frequently into a shared branch and running automated builds and tests on every change to catch problems early. Continuous Delivery (CD) extends CI so that every change that passes tests is automatically prepared and ready to deploy to production, but the final release is triggered by a manual approval. Continuous Deployment goes one step further: every change that passes all automated checks is deployed to production automatically with no human gate. The progression is CI (integrate and verify) to Delivery (always release-ready, human-approved) to Deployment (fully automated release).
questions.realTimeExample: In our project CI ran tests on every push, Delivery automatically deployed to staging for sign-off, and Deployment pushed to production whenever the release pipeline passed, so a merge could reach users within the hour.

questions.question: How do you set up GitLab CI build triggers on code push?
questions.answer: GitLab CI is configured with a `.gitlab-ci.yml` file at the repository root that defines stages, jobs, and the runner image to use. A pipeline is triggered automatically on every push or merge request; you control when jobs run using the `rules` or legacy `only`/`except` keywords. You can restrict jobs to specific branches, tags, or change paths, and register a GitLab Runner (shared or self-hosted) to execute them. Running tests on push is as simple as adding a job with a script that invokes your test command and a JUnit report for results, and GitLab displays the pipeline status directly on the commit and merge request.
questions.realTimeExample: We added a .gitlab-ci.yml with build and test stages, and every push to a merge-request branch automatically ran our suite while the merge request showed a green or red pipeline badge.
questions.code:
stages: [build, test]

build-job:
  stage: build
  image: maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17
  script:
    - mvn -B clean package -DskipTests

test-job:
  stage: test
  image: maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17
  script:
    - mvn -B test
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "push"'
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: target/surefire-reports/*.xml

questions.question: How do you connect your tests to Azure DevOps and configure pipeline triggers for pull requests?
questions.answer: In Azure DevOps I connect tests by defining a pipeline in a `azure-pipelines.yml` file (or via the classic designer) that restores dependencies, builds the code, and runs the test task, publishing results so they appear under the Tests tab. I use the PublishTestResults task with JUnit or VSTest format to surface pass and fail details on the pipeline run. To trigger on pull requests I enable the branch policy for the target branch and select the pipeline as a required build validation, so the pipeline runs automatically on every PR and can block merging until it passes. For CI on branches I set the `trigger` block, and for pull requests specifically I use the `pr` block with branch filters.
questions.realTimeExample: We required the Selenium pipeline as a build validation on pull requests to main, so no PR could be merged until the automated tests passed, and the test results showed up right inside the PR page.
questions.code:
trigger:
  branches:
    include: [ main, release/* ]

pr:
  branches:
    include: [ main ]

pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest

steps:
  - task: Maven@4
    inputs:
      goals: 'clean test'
  - task: PublishTestResults@2
    inputs:
      testResultsFormat: 'JUnit'
      testResultsFiles: '**/surefire-reports/*.xml'
    condition: always()

questions.question: How do you handle failed tests in a pipeline?
questions.answer: When a test fails in the pipeline, the first step is to capture and publish the reports and artifacts (logs, screenshots, videos, JUnit XML) so the failure is diagnosable, using something like `junit` in Jenkins or an artifact upload step. The pipeline should fail the build and mark the commit or pull request as failing so the change cannot be merged, which enforces quality gates. I distinguish between genuine product failures and flaky or environmental issues by re-running just the failed test and reviewing the evidence, then either fix the code, fix the flaky test, or quarantine it. Failures trigger notifications to the team channel, and repeat offenders are tracked in a backlog item rather than ignored, since letting red builds persist erodes trust in the suite.
questions.realTimeExample: When a UI test failed in Jenkins, the pipeline still published the JUnit report and the failure screenshot, so I could see it was a timing issue; I added an explicit wait, re-ran the job, and the build went green.

questions.question: Tests pass locally but fail (sometimes randomly) in CI - Jenkins, a Docker node or GitHub Actions. How do you investigate and debug?
questions.answer: First I recognize this is usually an environmental difference rather than a real product bug, so I compare the CI environment to my local one: OS, browser and driver versions, screen resolution, timezone, locale, installed dependencies, and available resources. Common culprits are missing or mismatched drivers, headless mode differences, slower or shared CI machines causing race conditions and timing flakiness, and tests depending on execution order or shared state. I make failures reproducible by capturing logs, screenshots, videos, and using the same Docker image locally, then fix root causes with explicit waits instead of sleeps, isolated test data, and deterministic selectors. I avoid simply retrying to hide flakiness; I stabilize the test and use retries only as a temporary safety net while tracking the underlying issue.
